subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit

note: RealityKit draws the scene itself and is the renderer Apple's own apps and system viewers use for USD content; the pass structure is not exposed, and the only developer hook into the frame is a post-process callback.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The graphics interface a runtime targets is a build choice inside one system, and an arriving asset cannot tell the difference.
note: The renderer targets Metal only. Custom shading is written in Metal, and a RealityKit scene can be driven inside an existing Metal workflow; there is no path to any other graphics interface.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: An asset that arrives against a different surface model still loads, but the further apart the two models are the more the look drifts.
note: Three material kinds ship: a physically based material that mirrors what USDZ carries, a shader-graph material built in Reality Composer Pro or loaded from MaterialX, and a custom material with Metal surface shaders and geometry modifiers.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A moved scene whose lights are read differently is lit wrong rather than lost.
note: Image-based lighting, directional, point and spot lights, baked lightmaps and diffuse probes are all in the framework. The trap for interchange: RealityKit ignores every light authored inside a USD file and lights the scene from the real room instead, so a lighting rig does not survive the move into this renderer.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Effects applied after the main pass are the receiving system's taste and carry nothing across.
note: A registered callback receives the finished frame before display, and bloom and tone mapping ship as components.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
capability: Level of detail and streaming order
interop_reason: Without an agreed order for what to send first, a large scene still arrives, it just pops and stalls on the way in.
note: There is no level-of-detail or streaming-order mechanism in either framework. Apple's own guidance is to do it by hand at authoring time: size each asset for how large it will appear and cut big meshes into pieces so off-camera parts can be culled.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Only content captured as splats is affected: a system that cannot draw them shows nothing of it, while mesh content is untouched.
note: RealityKit renders three-dimensional Gaussian splats through a dedicated component, with spherical-harmonic colour, sorting and projection modes. It reads no splat file: the app parses PLY, USD or any other container itself and fills GPU buffers, so there is no interchange path, only a rendering path.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The same holds for point clouds and volumetric video, which travel in forms few systems read.
note: Captured scenes reach the screen as splats, and stereoscopic and Apple Immersive Video play through a video component; a point cloud is drawn only inside the object-capture scanning view. There is no general voxel or point-cloud renderer and no volumetric video codec in the frameworks themselves.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Labels, signs and name tags lose their font and layout when the two systems disagree, so the text degrades while the rest of the asset is fine.
note: Text becomes an extruded mesh through a generator on the mesh resource, and USD assets can carry text through Apple's preliminary text schema.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Authored viewpoints are part of a scene, and losing them costs the arrival shot, not the scene.
note: In an AR session the device camera is the viewpoint; outside one, a perspective camera entity sets it, and RealityRenderer takes an explicit active camera.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: If the receiving system cannot rebuild the same tree, parenting and transforms collapse and the asset does not assemble at all.
note: The scene is an entity tree with components attached; Reality Composer Pro authors the same entity-component-system model that the runtime executes.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A disagreement about handedness or axis order puts every object in the wrong place or mirrored, which is the classic hand fix.
note: Every entity carries a transform of scale, rotation as a unit quaternion, and translation. The frame is Y-up and right-handed, which matches OpenUSD and glTF and differs from the left-handed engines.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The file is the boundary: if the second system cannot open it, nothing else on this list matters.
note: The container is OpenUSD: the loader reads .usd, .usda, .usdc, .usdz and Apple's own .reality file. RealityKit itself only loads; authoring USD is USDKit's job, and Object Capture and RoomPlan are the parts of the platform that write it.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A mesh encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a mesh, and the compression choice is where this usually breaks.
note: Geometry arrives as USD meshes, in text or binary form; procedural primitives, extruded paths and a low-level mesh with an app-defined vertex layout are all available at runtime.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Device-specific texture compression is the common failure: the model arrives untextured and someone must re-export it.
note: Textures load into GPU-resident resources with optional ASTC compression, and the USDZ archive is limited to four image encodings.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Carrying materials without loss is what "renders in another system" means, and only two subjects reach this row natively today.
note: MaterialX comes in, but not without loss. A shader-graph material can be built straight from MaterialX data, and Apple publishes the exact places RealityKit falls short of the specification: one packed texture per material, two UV sets, and only the first texture transform in a material is honoured.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A clip that cannot be read leaves the object still, and an avatar that cannot move is not an avatar.
note: Animation resources travel inside the asset file and are played, sequenced, grouped and looped at runtime; Reality Composer Pro adds multi-track sequences and an animation graph.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The bone hierarchy is what makes a body move correctly elsewhere; without an agreed one, motion has nothing to bind to.
note: A mesh carries a joint hierarchy and per-vertex joint influences, and the runtime exposes named skeletal poses for reading and writing. One constraint on the way in: Apple asks authors to merge several rigs into a single joint hierarchy before export.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Blend shapes carry facial detail, so losing them freezes a face rather than stopping the transfer.
note: Blend shape weights are a component whose named weight sets can be read and written at runtime.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A scene without agreed instancing still loads, it just costs far more memory and frames.
note: A component performs GPU instancing over one entity's model, and instancing of mesh and texture data survives import from USD.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Layered references are a working convenience, and flattening on export is the fallback that keeps the asset moving.
note: This is the strongest interchange story in the subject. Composition is USD's: files reference other files and override what they reference, USDKit exposes layers and stages to Swift, and a USD stage can be rendered straight into an entity hierarchy.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A metre read as a centimetre makes the asset useless on arrival, and rescaling by hand is the fix the use case forbids.
note: One unit is one metre, and the physics simulation states the same unit independently.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: An item that arrives with no readable terms cannot be lawfully worn, shown or sold, so the move fails at the rights boundary even when every byte arrives.
note: Nothing in ARKit, RealityKit or the USDZ packaging guidance carries terms of use with an asset. Apple's USD documentation covers geometry, materials, behaviour and packaging and says nothing about rights.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A signed record of who made an asset lets a receiver trust it; without one the asset still works but nobody can check its history.
note: There is no signed record of who made an asset and how. USDZ is a plain zip archive of a USD file and its dependencies, with no signature and no content credential.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The portable description of the body is the artefact this use case moves; with no agreement the person arrives as nothing.
note: The platform has an avatar — the spatial Persona a person appears as in a shared session — but the app never sees it. The system places and renders Personas; there is no portable body description, no file, and no app-side representation to move anywhere else.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Agreed bone names are what let animation authored anywhere play on the arriving body.
note: ARKit publishes one named joint hierarchy for tracked human bodies, with a stated neutral height, and a character has to be rigged to it to be driven. It is Apple's own list rather than an agreed interchange skeleton, and it exists for body tracking, not for carrying an avatar between worlds.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The use case names expressions, and named shapes the destination does not know leave a blank face.
note: ARKit's named blend-shape coefficients for the face are the closest thing the industry has to a shared expression vocabulary, and many other systems copy the names. They are a tracking output on iOS front-camera sessions, not a format, and Apple defines no viseme set for speech.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Retargeting is the repair when skeletons differ, so its absence costs motion quality rather than the visit.
note: A body-tracked entity plays a live person's motion on a virtual character, and a full-body inverse kinematics solver adapts a pose procedurally. Both require the character to be rigged to Apple's skeleton; there is no general mapping between two arbitrary rigs.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Equipped items are named in the use case, and attachment points that do not survive leave items on the floor or on the wrong bone.
note: No worn or carried item model, and no attachment-point convention for one. Anything worn is an ordinary child entity of the wearer's transform, with no named socket that would survive a move to another system.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Reduced forms matter for crowds and weak devices, and their absence costs frames, not presence.
note: No reduced avatar representation for crowds or weak devices. There is no level-of-detail mechanism of any kind in the frameworks.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Without a way to bind an avatar to a verifiable identity, the person who arrives cannot be shown to be the person who left.
note: Nothing binds an avatar to a checkable identity. A spatial Persona belongs to the Apple account on the call, and the app is given neither the Persona nor a credential about it.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Mass and velocity carried across make a moved object behave nearly the same; their absence changes the behaviour without stopping it.
note: A physics body component gives an entity mass and Newtonian response, and a separate motion component carries linear and angular velocity; a simulation component sets gravity and solver iterations for a subtree.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Collision shapes travel separately from visible geometry, and losing them means objects pass through each other until the destination builds its own.
note: Collision shapes are a separate component from the visible mesh and also serve queries, ray casts and convex shape casts; box, convex mesh and triangle mesh shapes are named explicitly.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Hinges and sliders that do not survive turn an assembly into loose parts, which is a loss of behaviour rather than of the asset.
note: Joints link two entities at named pin poses with linear and angular limits, and live on a joints component inside a simulation.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Friction and restitution numbers mean different things to different solvers, so agreeing on them buys little and each world may keep its own feel.
note: A physics material resource carries static friction, dynamic friction and restitution.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Two engines producing the same trajectory would let one object be simulated in two places at once, and nothing does that today.
note: Apple states no determinism guarantee for the simulation. The synchronised multi-device model is authority-and-replication over the network rather than a matching simulation on each device, which is the design a system without determinism has to choose.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Cloth and hair are the visible part, so a moved avatar arrives stiff rather than absent.
note: No cloth and no deformable body simulation is documented in either framework. Deformation is available only as skinning and blend shapes, which are animation, not simulation.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Regions that fire events are part of how content behaves, and their loss makes the content inert rather than unreadable.
note: A trigger volume is an invisible shape that reports entry and exit without taking part in the simulation, and any collision entity can be switched into trigger mode.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Positioned sounds are authored into a scene, and losing them leaves a silent room.
note: Sound is played from an entity and follows it; playback is spatial unless the app asks otherwise, and mix groups gather several playing sounds under one gain.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: How direction is turned into sound at the ears is the receiving system's method, like a rendering method.
note: Three rendering modes ship: spatial with distance attenuation and directivity, ambient projected from an angle without reverberation, and channel routed straight to the outputs. Spatial sources are mono only, so a multichannel asset is mixed down before spatialization.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A space's acoustic description is authored with it, and without agreement the room sounds wrong rather than silent.
note: On visionOS the real room is simulated by default and colours every spatial source; a reverb component overrides it with a named preset for an authored environment.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The receiving runtime works this out from its own geometry, frame by frame.
note: Surfaces have acoustic materials with per-band absorption and scattering, which is the input an occlusion model needs, and a named preset list covers common real surfaces. What is missing is the control: no documented obstruction or occlusion setting, and no way to ask whether geometry blocks a given source.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A visitor can be given audio by other means, so disagreement costs quality and scale.
note: An audio resource loads from a file or a URL and its loading strategy decides how the data is handled before and during playback, which covers reading a long asset without holding it in memory. There is no network audio delivery of the subject's own.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A visitor who cannot be heard is diminished but still present, and text remains a fallback.
note: Neither framework carries live voice. A shared session on this platform runs on a FaceTime call, and the call carries the talking; the app gets synchronised activity data, not an audio channel it can route into the scene.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A client or agent that cannot read the destination's state stream arrives blind, which ends both use cases on the spot.
note: Every entity has a synchronization component with a network identifier, and the multipeer service keeps the scenes of connected devices matching automatically. It is same-app replication: both ends run the same build of the same app.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Disagreement about who owns an arriving object shows up as rubber-banding and contested edits rather than as a failed arrival.
note: One process owns an entity, the owner can be read, ownership can be handed to a named peer, and a transfer mode governs whether a request is granted.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Without agreement the destination sends everything or too little, which costs scale.
note: Nothing decides what each peer needs. The multipeer session synchronises the scene to all connected devices, and no filter, relevance rule or area of interest is exposed.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Latency hiding is local repair work, so its absence is felt as lag.
note: No prediction and no reconciliation. Apple's own guidance is that synchronisation can simply fail on a poor connection, with no local-correction machinery offered.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: With no shared wire protocol there is no session to join at all.
note: The one transport the subject ships is peer-to-peer: RealityKit's synchronization service is built on Multipeer Connectivity, which runs over infrastructure Wi-Fi, peer-to-peer Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. There is no client-server transport and no internet-scale session.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Live audio and video degrade or drop out while the visit continues.
note: Live video reaches the scene, but the transport is not the subject's. A video component takes a player the app supplies and draws its output in three dimensions; nothing in ARKit or RealityKit moves an audio or video stream between participants.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Joining a running world, authentication included, is the door: no agreement, no entry.
note: Joining is done by two other frameworks. Nearby devices invite each other through Multipeer Connectivity, and a shared session across a call is a SharePlay group activity on the FaceTime infrastructure. RealityKit adds only a compatibility check so a host can refuse a peer on an incompatible version.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: This row is the portal itself, and the travel use case is nothing but the handoff.
note: There is no leaving one world and arriving in another with state intact. RealityKit's portal looks into a second world inside the same app's scene, and entities may cross its boundary, but both worlds belong to one process; nothing crosses to another publisher's experience.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A roster that does not cross operators means you cannot see who is where, but you can still be there.
note: Within one collaborative session ARKit reports an anchor for each nearby user, giving their pose, and a group activity has a participant list. Both stop at the edge of the session; there is no roster across operators or across apps.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A destination name that does not resolve cannot be travelled to, so naming and resolution are the first agreement.
note: No world is named and no name is resolved. The only address in the subject is a file address: a web page links a USDZ or Reality file and the system opens it in AR Quick Look, which names a model, not a place.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Worlds can be reached by a known address, so discovery adds reach rather than making it possible.
note: Discovery is Multipeer Connectivity's: a browser looks for nearby devices advertising a named service type, and the app must declare the Bonjour services it browses. It reaches the local network only.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A shared clock keeps events in order; without one the ordering drifts and coarse clocks still hold the session together.
note: No shared clock. Frames carry a local capture timestamp and the physics simulation can be driven by a custom clock, but neither is agreed between devices, and nothing orders events across a session.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: With no shared base identifier the same person or agent is a stranger in every world they enter.
note: Neither framework defines an identifier for a person, agent or thing. Identity on this platform lives in separate sign-in services outside the subject.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Claims about age, membership or ownership are worthless if the receiving world cannot read them.
note: No format for a checkable claim about a subject, and nothing in either framework reads one.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A credential nobody can ask for or present is not a credential, and one subject reaches this row natively today.
note: No protocol for requesting and presenting claims.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A world that cannot read what an arriving person or agent is allowed to do must either refuse it or trust it blindly.
note: There is a permission model, but it is app-to-system and not portable: a session asks the person for world-sensing or hand-tracking authorization and the system answers. Nothing states what a subject may do in a form a second party could check.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Without selective disclosure the traveller over-shares, which is a harm rather than a stop.
note: Selective disclosure of credentials is not something either framework does. The platform's privacy work is of a different kind: it withholds sensor data from the app rather than revealing part of a claim to a receiver.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Relationships and standing that do not travel leave the person present but unknown.
note: No relationships and no standing are modelled.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The terms themselves must cross, and that row is a must; acting on them is the receiver's own behaviour, and no agreed mechanism exists yet.
note: Nothing acts on licence terms at the point of use, because nothing carries them.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Content pinned to the Earth must land in the same place in the other system, and a pose that cannot be read puts it somewhere else.
note: A location anchor is placed by latitude, longitude and optional altitude, and the session keeps its position and orientation as the user moves, aligned East-North-Up.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A frame disagreement is measured in metres or kilometres, not in taste.
note: One frame, fixed. Coordinates are latitude and longitude in WGS 84 with altitude in metres against sea level, and the local frame is East-North-Up. There is no way to name a different reference system, and no transformation machinery.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: An anchor made on one device never leaves it; the sharing case is the next row.
note: Anchors are the core primitive on both device families: an ARKit anchor fixes a transform in the session's world space on iOS, and a world anchor does the same on visionOS, with a RealityKit anchor entity tethering content to a plane, image or fixed point.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Two people in two systems must see the same thing in the same spot, and today one subject reaches this row, through an extension.
note: Three routes, all first-party. A world map serialises the mapped space and its anchors so a second device can relocalise into it; a collaborative session streams the same knowledge continuously; and on visionOS a world anchor can be created shared with nearby participants, with a provider that establishes a shared coordinate space. Persistence across runs is stated for world anchors.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Recovering pose from imagery can fall back to satellite position and manual alignment, at worse accuracy.
note: ARKit recovers precise pose from camera imagery by matching the live frame against Apple's own street-level localization imagery, downloaded for the area around the user's satellite position. Two limits the map should record: outdoors only, and only where Apple has captured imagery.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: City-scale data is streamed by tile, and a tileset the receiving client cannot stream has to be converted before it is usable.
note: No tiled terrain or city streaming. Location anchors carry no geometry, and Apple's guidance for large scenes is to split meshes by hand rather than to stream by tile.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A structured description of an interior makes placement and routing better; without one both are cruder, and nothing reaches this row today.
note: ARKit itself classifies detected planes as floor, wall, ceiling, door, window, table or seat, which is a start but not a room description. The structured interior comes from a separate framework, RoomPlan, which scans a room into parametric data and exports it as USD.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The visitor's app and the device runtime are two independent systems, and if they cannot start an immersive session the visit does not happen.
note: Both device families have an explicit session object. On iOS a session runs a configuration that decides what is tracked; on visionOS a session runs data providers and asks for the matching authorizations, and RealityKit wraps the visionOS side in a spatial tracking session.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A world that reads controllers differently is harder to use, and pointer and text paths remain.
note: Neither ARKit nor RealityKit defines controller input. The platform's Game Controller framework supplies it, with one spatial rule worth recording: a visionOS app receives controller events only while the person is looking at its window.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Hand tracking adds a way in, and its absence falls back to controllers.
note: A hand-tracking provider streams hand and joint positions, and RealityKit can ask for hand anchoring through its spatial tracking session. It is gated: the person must grant hand-tracking authorization, and the app must be showing an immersive space.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Gaze is an aid with privacy limits, and everything works without it.
note: The two halves of the platform answer this oppositely, and the difference matters for any standard that assumes app-readable gaze. On iOS a face anchor gives eye transforms and an estimated look-at point. On visionOS gaze is never given to the app at all: the system applies focus and hover on the person's behalf and tells the app only that something was tapped.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Touch feedback is felt when it is missing, and nothing stops.
note: No haptics in either framework. The platform's Core Haptics framework composes patterns, documented for iOS apps and for supported game controllers.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A world that cannot ask what the arriving device can do will guess, and guessing wrong costs quality rather than entry.
note: Capability discovery is explicit and per-feature on both sides: an iOS configuration class answers whether the device supports it, and each visionOS data provider type answers the same question for the current runtime.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The language a world writes its rules in is its own business and never has to cross.
note: Two runtimes, and the second is new. World rules are ordinarily written in Swift as systems over the entity-component model. Since Reality Composer Pro 3 they can instead be authored as Script Graphs, attached to entities as a scripting component, published inside the Reality file with the content, and run by an open-source Swift package.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The use case says the asset must behave, so a door that will not open in the second system is the failure this row names.
note: Interactivity travels with the asset. Apple's preliminary USD schemas add actions and triggers so a USD file can react to real-world situations, and a Script Graph ships inside a Reality file with the entities it drives. The caution is the word preliminary, which Apple applies to these schemas itself.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A host can sandbox guest content on its own; agreement only makes the limits predictable for the guest.
note: There is no guest-content model to sandbox. Assets are loaded as data and Script Graph logic runs in the app's own process through a linked Swift package; nothing runs untrusted code with limits.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: An agent with no agreed way to perceive and act in a world it did not come from cannot join it at all.
note: Reality Composer Pro 3 adds the parts an autonomous character needs — behaviour trees, an animation state machine and a navigation mesh with path finding — and Apple names character intelligence as a feature of the release. These are authored non-player characters inside one app, not agents that arrive from elsewhere or act across worlds.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Without agreed limits, guest content and agents are throttled or refused unpredictably.
note: Nothing bounds memory, time or calls for content the app did not write. The only documented ceiling is one the framework enforces on itself — a cap on splat count whose initializer throws — and there is no API to set a budget.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: What survives a restart is mostly the host's business; it crosses the boundary only when a visitor's changes must last.
note: What survives a restart is the map of the room, not the world. A world map serialises the session's space-mapping state and its anchors and can be reloaded into a new session, and visionOS persists world anchors across runs. Entity state, ownership and scene contents are the app's own problem.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The use case names inventory, and items that cannot be read at the destination do not travel with the person.
note: Neither framework models items a person holds. There is no inventory to travel.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: The use case names preferences, and for a person who depends on comfort and accessibility settings, arriving without them ends the visit.
note: Settings and accessibility choices belong to the device and follow the person across apps on that device only; nothing carries them to another operator's experience, and neither framework exposes them as portable data.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Naming content by hash makes an item the same item everywhere; without it copies drift while still loading.
note: Content is referred to by bundle name or file address, never by hash. The loading methods take a name in a bundle or a file URL, and USDZ references its dependencies by path inside the archive.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A runnable experience moves between hosts far less often than an asset does, and repackaging is the fallback.
note: USDZ is the packaging answer and it is a real one: a zip archive holding the USD file and every dependency, opened by the system viewer from an app or from a web link, with .reality as the alternative when Apple's authoring tool wrote the scene.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Assets reach clients over ordinary web delivery, so agreement here buys scale and cost rather than possibility.
note: There is no delivery mechanism of the subject's own. Assets come from the app bundle or a file address, and the only remote path is a plain web link to a single USDZ file that the system opens in AR Quick Look. Nothing streams, negotiates or caches at scale.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A reader that cannot tell which version it holds, or what to do with the parts it does not know, breaks on the first update, which is the "no hand fixes" test again.
note: Versioning is by operating-system release, and the subject is honest about the breakage. Peers on incompatible RealityKit versions cannot synchronise and a token exists so a host can refuse them. On the content side Apple warns that its preliminary schemas can change at any time and should not be relied on across releases, and the current authoring tool removed its own predecessor outright.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: Every other must row is a claim until a shared test says it holds, which is exactly what the meeting asked for.
note: There is structural validation and there is a published feature matrix, but no conformance suite. Apple points authors at OpenUSD's usdchecker for well-formedness, says plainly that it does not catch visual or behavioural problems, and publishes per-renderer support tables so an author can see what four different Apple renderers will and will not read from the same file. Nothing proves an implementation matches a specification.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
capability: World generation from a prompt or an image
interop_reason: A generated place that arrives only as frames to watch still reaches the viewer, but as a recording rather than a world the receiver can open and use.
note: Apple's ARKit and RealityKit are a device platform: the frameworks a phone or headset application uses to see the room and draw in it, and making a whole three-dimensional place from a description or a picture is not an act it performs or specifies.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: A world continued by a model still reaches a viewer, but only as what the model chooses to show, so the receiver cannot keep it or run it again.
note: Apple's ARKit and RealityKit are a device platform: the frameworks a phone or headset application uses to see the room and draw in it, and it never continues a world under a viewer's actions from a learned model; there is no such model here.

subject: Apple ARKit and RealityKit
interop_reason: How a system turns photographs into a model is its own method, and what leaves is an ordinary asset the container and geometry rows already carry.
note: Turning a set of ordinary photographs of a real object into a textured model is a shipped first-party service, named as photogrammetry in Apple's own words, available on the phone and on the desktop. This is the clearest native claim on this row anywhere on the map.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR

The platform tracks the user's own body by inferring joint positions from the head and hands with inverse kinematics, and tracks hand joints under the OpenXR conventions, but neither is a naming or structure agreement for a character rig that would let animation transfer between worlds.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: The use case names expressions, and named shapes the destination does not know leave a blank face.

On a headset, face tracking returns 68 blend shape values with Google's own names, in the style of facial action coding, each between nought and one, with confidence for three regions. On a phone, Augmented Faces instead returns a 468-point dense mesh with a centre pose and three region poses. Neither is an interchange format: the documentation defines the values and gives no mapping to any published expression or viseme set, so another world needs a conversion table nobody has published, and the two halves do not even agree with each other.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Retargeting is the repair when skeletons differ, so its absence costs motion quality rather than the visit.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Equipped items are named in the use case, and attachment points that do not survive leave items on the floor or on the wrong bone.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Reduced forms matter for crowds and weak devices, and their absence costs frames, not presence.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Without a way to bind an avatar to a verifiable identity, the person who arrives cannot be shown to be the person who left.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Mass and velocity carried across make a moved object behave nearly the same; their absence changes the behaviour without stopping it.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Collision shapes travel separately from visible geometry, and losing them means objects pass through each other until the destination builds its own.
note: No collision shapes of its own, though it supplies the raw material for someone else's: depth maps of the real room, detected planes with their outlines, and scene meshes of physical objects, all of which an app's own physics engine can collide against.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Hinges and sliders that do not survive turn an assembly into loose parts, which is a loss of behaviour rather than of the asset.
note: No joints or constraints, because there is no simulation to constrain.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Friction and restitution numbers mean different things to different solvers, so agreeing on them buys little and each world may keep its own feel.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Two engines producing the same trajectory would let one object be simulated in two places at once, and nothing does that today.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Cloth and hair are the visible part, so a moved avatar arrives stiff rather than absent.
note: No soft bodies or cloth anywhere in the platform.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Regions that fire events are part of how content behaves, and their loss makes the content inert rather than unreadable.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Positioned sounds are authored into a scene, and losing them leaves a silent room.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: How direction is turned into sound at the ears is the receiving system's method, like a rendering method.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A space's acoustic description is authored with it, and without agreement the room sounds wrong rather than silent.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: The receiving runtime works this out from its own geometry, frame by frame.
note: Nothing muffles or blocks a sound by geometry, even though the platform knows the geometry: it detects planes and can mesh the room, and none of that reaches the audio path.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A visitor can be given audio by other means, so disagreement costs quality and scale.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Disagreement about who owns an arriving object shows up as rubber-banding and contested edits rather than as a failed arrival.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Without agreement the destination sends everything or too little, which costs scale.
note: No interest management. Nothing is being sent to a client to be filtered.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Latency hiding is local repair work, so its absence is felt as lag.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: With no shared wire protocol there is no session to join at all.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Live audio and video degrade or drop out while the visit continues.
note: Media arrives, media never leaves. The runtime plays streamed stereoscopic and multi-view video and streamed audio through the ordinary Android media stack, and the live connection to Gemini carries audio in both directions, but there is no participant media path.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Joining a running world, authentication included, is the door: no agreement, no entry.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: This row is the portal itself, and the travel use case is nothing but the handoff.
note: No portals and no handoff. Leaving one experience means leaving one Android application; nothing carries state across that boundary.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A roster that does not cross operators means you cannot see who is where, but you can still be there.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A destination name that does not resolve cannot be travelled to, so naming and resolution are the first agreement.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Worlds can be reached by a known address, so discovery adds reach rather than making it possible.
note: Nothing discovers worlds, nodes or services. The only catalogue is the app store: a person browses Google Play on the headset and installs an application.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A shared clock keeps events in order; without one the ordering drifts and coarse clocks still hold the session together.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: With no shared base identifier the same person or agent is a stranger in every world they enter.
note: A device platform with no account model of its own for content. Identity here is the Google account on the device and the Google Cloud project behind an application, neither of which is a portable identifier for a person or an agent in a world.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Claims about age, membership or ownership are worthless if the receiving world cannot read them.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A credential nobody can ask for or present is not a credential, and one subject reaches this row natively today.
note: No credential presentation protocol between parties. The one exchange that exists is an application authenticating itself to Google, with a token signed by a service account.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A world that cannot read what an arriving person or agent is allowed to do must either refuse it or trust it blindly.

Every sensitive perception feature is gated by an Android runtime permission the person grants on the device — hand tracking, face tracking, eye tracking, coarse and fine scene understanding — and nothing about that grant can be read by a party that did not issue it.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Without selective disclosure the traveller over-shares, which is a harm rather than a stop.
note: No selective disclosure in the credential sense. The platform's only disclosure control is the per-sensor runtime permission, which decides what one application on one device may see and carries nothing to anywhere else.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Relationships and standing that do not travel leave the person present but unknown.
note: No reputation and no social graph. The platform has no notion of a relationship between two people.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: The terms themselves must cross, and that row is a must; acting on them is the receiver's own behaviour, and no agreed mechanism exists yet.
note: No rights enforcement at the point of use for content. Rights here bind the developer, not the asset: the additional terms restrict what may be built on the cloud anchor and geospatial interfaces, and the app store binds the buyer, while nothing is checked when a model is drawn.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Content pinned to the Earth must land in the same place in the other system, and a pose that cannot be read puts it somewhere else.
note: This is the platform's strongest row. The Geospatial interface returns the device's pose against the Earth — latitude, longitude, altitude and an orientation — with an accuracy estimate for each, and any pose in the local session can be converted to and from that Earth-referenced form. Note the frame: the orientation is expressed east, up and south, which is Google's own convention and not the one the Open Geospatial Consortium's pose standard uses, and there is no exchange encoding for it at all.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A frame disagreement is measured in metres or kilometres, not in taste.
note: One reference system, fixed, with a known seam. Horizontal position follows the world geodetic system of 1984 and altitude is metres above that ellipsoid, so ground level is not zero; the documentation itself tells developers to convert an elevation obtained from Google's own maps interface, which uses a gravity-based geoid, before comparing it. There is no way to state or negotiate a different reference system.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: An anchor made on one device never leaves it; the sharing case is the next row.
note: Fixing content to a place on one device is the core of both halves. On a phone an anchor holds a pose steady as tracking is refitted, and content can also be pinned to a printed image, with up to twenty tracked at once out of a database of up to a thousand. On a headset an anchor can be created free-standing or attached to a tracked plane, and it can be persisted into the app's own private storage under an identifier and reloaded in a later session.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Two people in two systems must see the same thing in the same spot, and today one subject reaches this row, through an extension.
note: Shared across devices on phones, and not on headsets — the same product name covers two different capabilities. A Cloud Anchor uploads a feature map to Google's endpoint, returns an identifier, and lets an Android or an Apple device in the same room resolve the same place later, with an expiry time that can be extended up to a stated maximum. On Android XR there is no cloud anchor: persistence is to the app's private storage, and the sharing extension shares an anchor with other applications running on the same device.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Recovering pose from imagery can fall back to satellite position and manual alignment, at worse accuracy.
note: Visual positioning is the reason this subject belongs on the map. Camera pixels are matched against a localization model built from more than fifteen years of Street View imagery, combined into a global point cloud of trillions of points, and the result is a device pose far better than satellite positioning alone. It is a service, not a specification, and the terms of use are part of the capability: you cannot point it at another provider's map, the additional terms forbid building anything that re-creates the features of another Google product, and they bar both the visual positioning interface and cloud anchors from services directed at children.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: City-scale data is streamed by tile, and a tileset the receiving client cannot stream has to be converted before it is usable.
note: City-scale geometry is streamed, but not as tiles anyone else can read. Streetscape Geometry hands the app meshes of terrain and buildings around the user, derived from Street View, graded by the levels of detail defined in the CityGML standard. They arrive as tracked objects inside a session with vertex and index buffers, never as a tileset with a manifest, so nothing else can consume them and they cannot be cached or served on.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A structured description of an interior makes placement and routing better; without one both are cruder, and nothing reaches this row today.
note: Interiors are described, loosely. On a headset, detected planes carry a semantic label — wall, floor, ceiling or table — with a centre pose, extents in metres and a bounding polygon, and a scene meshing extension approximates the physical objects in the room. That is a running description for one app in one room, not a structured model of a building, and the outdoor semantic labelling on phones states outright that it is not meant for interiors.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: The visitor's app and the device runtime are two independent systems, and if they cannot start an immersive session the visit does not happen.
note: Immersive session lifecycle is exactly what both halves provide. A perception session is created, configured feature by feature and reconfigured while running, and every capability — device tracking, planes, depth, hands, faces, anchor persistence — is off until the app asks for it and the person grants the matching permission.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A world that reads controllers differently is harder to use, and pointer and text paths remain.
note: Six-degrees-of-freedom motion controllers are supported through OpenXR, tracked for position and movement, with directional pad and button bindings for actions and hover.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Hand tracking adds a way in, and its absence falls back to controllers.
note: Articulated hand tracking is first class and is the default way to interact. Each hand has a tracking state and a map of joints to poses, and the joint definitions are the OpenXR ones rather than a private set, which is what makes the data portable.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Gaze is an aid with privacy limits, and everything works without it.
note: Eye tracking gives the position and orientation of the user's eyes through a vendor extension, guarded by its own runtime permission, and gaze can also be used directly as an interaction: looking at a thing and selecting it.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Touch feedback is felt when it is missing, and nothing stops.
note: Uneven and, on phones, discouraged. A headset controller gets whatever OpenXR's core haptic output provides, since the runtime is conformant to version 1.1, but the platform documents no haptic feature of its own, and ARCore's own performance guidance tells developers to avoid haptic feedback because the vibration disturbs pose estimation.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A world that cannot ask what the arriving device can do will guess, and guessing wrong costs quality rather than entry.
note: Learning what the client can do is a first-class API in three places: spatial capabilities can be queried at any moment and change as the person moves the app between windowed and full space; depth support is queried per rendering mode before use; and the app manifest declares which extended reality feature set an app needs so the store only offers it to devices that have it.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: The language a world writes its rules in is its own business and never has to cross.
note: There is no world scripting language, because a world here is an Android application. Rules are compiled code shipped through a store, or a web page running in Chrome; neither is a script that travels with a scene.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: The use case says the asset must behave, so a door that will not open in the second system is the failure this row names.
note: No behaviour graphs and no declarative interactivity that travels with an asset. The supported glTF extension list has no interactivity extension in it, so a model arrives as geometry, materials and animation clips and nothing else.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A host can sandbox guest content on its own; agreement only makes the limits predictable for the guest.
note: Isolation is the strongest thing this platform inherits from Android. Every application gets its own user identity and process, and the kernel enforces the boundary between applications and the system; on top of that, every perception feature is behind a runtime permission, and a persisted anchor is stored in the app's private data where no other app can read it.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: An agent with no agreed way to perceive and act in a world it did not come from cannot join it at all.
note: An autonomous agent is built into the platform rather than added to it. Google describes Android XR as the first Android built in the Gemini era, with an assistant that understands what the user is looking at and acts for them, and apps reach the same models through Firebase, including a live conversational connection with function calling so the agent can drive the app.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Without agreed limits, guest content and agents are throttled or refused unpredictably.
note: Bounds exist but are advisory or external. An application can give performance hints to the runtime and read back frame times, utilization and frequency, and the store applies a hard download size limit, with asset delivery offered as the way around it. Nothing bounds memory, time or calls for guest content inside a running experience, because there is no guest content.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: What survives a restart is mostly the host's business; it crosses the boundary only when a visitor's changes must last.
note: What survives a restart is places, not worlds. An anchor can be persisted under an identifier into the app's private storage and reloaded later, and a Cloud Anchor survives on Google's endpoint until its expiry time, which can be pushed out to a stated maximum. Everything else in the scene is the app's own problem.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: The use case names inventory, and items that cannot be read at the destination do not travel with the person.
note: No inventory. The platform holds no items on a person's behalf; purchases are app store entitlements to applications, not things carried into a scene.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: The use case names preferences, and for a person who depends on comfort and accessibility settings, arriving without them ends the visit.
note: Preferences do not follow content. The system holds the person's own environment preference and restores it after another app has changed it, which is device-local state; nothing about accessibility or comfort settings travels with the user to another world.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Naming content by hash makes an item the same item everywhere; without it copies drift while still loading.
note: Nothing is addressed by hash. A model is named by a path, a uniform resource identifier or raw bytes, and a persisted anchor is named by an identifier the runtime hands out, which is a location in the app's own storage rather than a digest of anything.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A runnable experience moves between hosts far less often than an asset does, and repackaging is the fallback.
note: The runnable package is the Android App Bundle: compiled code and resources uploaded once, with the store generating and signing the actual package for each device configuration.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Assets reach clients over ordinary web delivery, so agreement here buys scale and cost rather than possibility.
note: Delivery is Google Play, all the way to the headset, with asset delivery for large amounts of content and feature delivery for parts that download on demand or conditionally.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A reader that cannot tell which version it holds, or what to do with the parts it does not know, breaks on the first update, which is the "no hand fixes" test again.
note: Versioning is the Android release machinery, extended for this platform: two release tracks, a manifest feature declaration that decides which devices are offered the build, and a runtime whose own version moves under the app — ARCore ships as a Google Play service and the current release is 1.56.0. The two halves are at different stages, which a version column cannot show: the headset platform is on sale while its software kit is still at Developer Preview 4.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Every other must row is a claim until a shared test says it holds, which is exactly what the meeting asked for.
note: Conformance is real on one side and closed on the other. Android XR is listed by Khronos as a conformant product for OpenXR versions 1.0 and 1.1, submitted by Google, so an app can test its assumptions against a published specification. ARCore's device requirements are the opposite: certification exists, and the complete list of requirements sits behind an original equipment manufacturer portal that is only available to authorized manufacturers, so nobody outside can prove a device meets it.

note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and making a whole three-dimensional place from a description or a picture is not an act it performs or specifies.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR

note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and it never continues a world under a viewer's actions from a learned model; there is no such model here.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: How a system turns photographs into a model is its own method, and what leaves is an ordinary asset the container and geometry rows already carry.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR

note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and it delivers no captured scene, progressively by region and detail or otherwise.

interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a volumetric clip is an asset like any other: without the calibration and mask metadata a second implementation needs, what arrives is not the recording and no one can make it one by hand.
note: Video in three dimensions plays and volumetric video does not. Stereoscopic playback is a pair of views, not a captured three-dimensional scene, and no calibration or mask metadata accompanies it.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a point cloud encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a point cloud, exactly as an undecodable mesh is not a mesh, and that capture shows nothing.
note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and it defines no encoding or compression for a set of points with attributes.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Making an image from a viewpoint no camera occupied is a method inside one system, and what crosses to a second system is the picture it produced.
note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and it produces no image from a viewing position that no capture camera occupied.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a moving capture handed over as unrelated frames is not the capture: the receiver has to guess the rate and the ordering the sender already knew, and guessing is the hand fix the use case forbids.
note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and it carries no captured scene that changes over time, and states no rate at which one should be played back.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Whether a captured scene answers the light around it is work the receiving system does, and the asset arrives either way.
note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and it holds no captured scene that could be made to answer the light of the place it lands in.

note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and there is no capture here to crop, delete from or recolour, and no export for such an edit to survive.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Describing a change to a world you already made is one service's own interface, and the world that results still leaves by the ordinary export rows.
note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and there is no generated world here to change by describing the change or pointing at a region.

interop_reason: A generator that cannot read the specification another tool wrote still produces a world, it just will not be the world that was asked for.
note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and nothing here accepts a specification of a world that should be made.

capability: Deriving conventional assets from a generated scene
interop_reason: Derived meshes and panoramas are how a generated world reaches a conventional engine at all, and each route loses something the receiver has to be told about.
note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and it derives no collision mesh, drawing mesh, panorama or video from a splat or radiance-field world.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: Actions that arrive without their embodiment, frame and units cannot be replayed elsewhere, so an agent acts only in the system it was written for.
note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and it carries no agent's actions in or out as time-sampled data with an embodiment, a frame and units.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A panorama whose projection is not stated is still an image, but the receiver has to guess before it can use it as a backdrop or as a light.
note: Google's ARCore and Android XR are a device platform whose two halves are a phone runtime and a headset runtime, and it carries no full 360-degree view of a place as an image with its projection stated.

subject: Google ARCore and Android XR
interop_reason: A reconstruction that cannot leave the device that made it keeps the room private to one session, so anything placed against it has to be fitted again elsewhere.
note: The room comes back as planes, not as a mesh.
