This is a genuinely uniform reflective model, but it is entirely Resonite's own; there is no published mapping onto any external scene-graph standard.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A disagreement about handedness or axis order puts every object in the wrong place or mirrored, which is the classic hand fix.
note: Resonite uses a LEFT-handed, Y-up, +Z-forward frame, matching Unity. glTF — the format Resonite imports most cleanly — is right-handed with -Z forward, so every transform, rotation sign and winding order has to be flipped on the way in and on the way out. Rotations are quaternions internally. Positions, rotations and scales live on every slot whether or not it renders anything.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: The file is the boundary: if the second system cannot open it, nothing else on this list matters.
note: Resonite's own container is `.resonitepackage`, a ZIP holding record files plus an Assets folder of SHA256-named blobs. It is documented, and it is explicitly a distribution format — but the docs state outright that compatibility with Unity packages and with other VR platforms is a NON-goal, and that it is not meant to be produced by third-party tools. So it carries Resonite content out of Resonite for backup and re-import into Resonite, and nothing else. The raw data-model file is `.brson`: Brotli-compressed BSON, no assets embedded.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A mesh encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a mesh, and the compression choice is where this usually breaks.
note: Every mesh that enters Resonite is converted to Resonite's own MeshX representation and the link to the source file is dropped. MeshX has no published specification and the code that reads and writes it is closed — `Elements.Assets` and `FrooxEngine` are not public repositories. On the way out, the export wizard offers Collada and OBJ only; FBX is listed as currently disabled and glTF is not offered at all. Exported skinned meshes lose bone weights and shape keys, which Resonite's own docs concede. Draco is explicitly unsupported on import, which is also why VRM 1.x cannot be loaded, and meshopt appears nowhere in the documentation.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Device-specific texture compression is the common failure: the model arrives untextured and someone must re-export it.
note: Image import goes through FreeImage and covers a very wide format list, and the same library is used for texture export, so most common image formats round-trip. Internally Resonite re-encodes: lossless WebP for destructive edits on standard images, EXR for high-bit-depth. GPU texture compression is done with AMD Compressonator and Crunch forks. DDS is read-only. KTX2 / Basis are not documented.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Carrying materials without loss is what "renders in another system" means, and only two subjects reach this row natively today.
note: There is no material exchange format. Because model formats disagree about PBR, Resonite works around it with a filename convention: put textures next to the model named `_albedo`, `_normal`, `_metallic` and so on, and the importer wires them into a material. That is a local heuristic, not an interchange mechanism, and it only works for single-material models each in their own folder. Nothing carries material definitions back out.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A clip that cannot be read leaves the object still, and an avatar that cannot move is not an avatar.
note: Resonite has its own animation formats: AnimX, a raw binary format with an "AnimX" magic word and optional LZ4 or LZMA encoding, and AnimJ, a JSON authoring format that must be imported and converted to AnimX before it can be used. AnimJ is a genuine third-party authoring route — you can write animation as JSON outside Resonite and bring it in. But neither has a vendor-published specification: the AnimX binary layout on the wiki is community reverse-engineering, `Elements.Assets` is not a public repository, and there is no AnimX repo in the Yellow Dog Man organisation. Bezier tracks are documented as not yet supported.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: The bone hierarchy is what makes a body move correctly elsewhere; without an agreed one, motion has nothing to bind to.
note: Skeletons come in through Assimp from FBX, glTF or Blender and are mapped by name heuristics into Resonite's BodyNode enum, stored on a BipedRig component as a dictionary from body node to slot. Bones do survive an export to `.resonitepackage`. There is no way to write a skeleton back out to an interchange format — the model export wizard offers Collada and OBJ, and OBJ carries no rig at all.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Blend shapes carry facial detail, so losing them freezes a face rather than stopping the transfer.
note: Blend shapes are supported and are the mechanism behind visemes and facial expressions, with heuristic auto-assignment by name. They are also called out in the optimisation guidance as a cost. As with meshes, they enter through Assimp and cannot be written back out to an interchange format.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A scene without agreed instancing still loads, it just costs far more memory and frames.
note: GPU mesh instancing happens automatically where a static mesh and material combination repeats, and the docs are specific about what defeats it: skinned mesh renderers are never instanced, and differing material property blocks break instancing across copies. Procedural assets are not instanced across copies; baking them to static meshes enables instancing and lets one copy live in memory.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Layered references are a working convenience, and flattening on export is the fallback that keeps the asset moving.
note: There is no layering, referencing or override system in the sense of composed scenes. A world is one slot tree; a record can reference other records, and public folders let one owner publish an item everyone else links to and receives updates for, which is the closest thing to a live reference. But there is no override mechanism, and Resonite's Limitations page notes there is no generic dynamic component or property access to build one on.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A metre read as a centimetre makes the asset useless on arrival, and rescaling by hand is the fix the use case forbids.
note: Resonite is metre-scaled, and says so — but only in one sentence, on a community-written avatar guide, not on any core reference page. The importer does not normalise scale for you: the user is told to export at the correct unit scale from their authoring tool. So the convention exists and matches glTF's metre convention, but it is not stated anywhere authoritative enough to build against.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: An item that arrives with no readable terms cannot be lawfully worn, shown or sold, so the move fails at the rights boundary even when every byte arrives.
note: Assets carry no licence or rights metadata. The wiki's own guidance on protecting your work says in-app obfuscation is easy to defeat, and points at two unimplemented GitHub roadmap issues — "Hard Permissions" and "Object ID / Licenses" — as the future answer. So this is openly acknowledged as missing.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A signed record of who made an asset lets a receiver trust it; without one the asset still works but nobody can check its history.
note: Cloud records record an owner and a record ID, so there is an authorship claim attached to anything saved to the cloud. It is an account-level ownership field on the operator's own database, not a signed provenance record, and it does not survive export into a `.resonitepackage` in any verifiable form.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: The portable description of the body is the artefact this use case moves; with no agreement the person arrives as nothing.
note: There is no portable avatar description. An avatar is an ordinary Resonite slot hierarchy with Resonite components on it, saved as a record or a `.resonitepackage`. Resonite READS FBX, glTF and Blender rigs and turns them into its own structure; it cannot WRITE any avatar format back out, and VRM — the one widely adopted portable avatar standard — is explicitly not supported on import. Community tooling converts VRM to `.resonitepackage` outside the platform.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Agreed bone names are what let animation authored anywhere play on the arriving body.
note: Resonite does not require an agreed bone standard — it guesses. On import it runs case-insensitive, substring-tolerant name heuristics ("cheese_hips" resolves to the hip bone) and fills in its own `BodyNode` enum, which is close to but not the same as Unity's HumanBodyBones: it adds Root, View, LeftController, RightController, palms and per-finger tips. The heuristic is what makes rigs built for other platforms work, so in practice it interoperates well, but nothing is guaranteed and there is no declared bone standard to conform to. Digitigrade legs are not supported.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: The use case names expressions, and named shapes the destination does not know leave a blank face.
note: Two halves, and they point opposite ways. Visemes ARE an external set: Resonite's Viseme enum is index-for-index the Oculus/OVR LipSync fifteen, proven by Yellow Dog Man's own OVRCompat source. Facial EXPRESSIONS are not: Resonite ships roughly ninety proprietary AvatarExpression names and deliberately does not adopt ARKit or VRCFT Unified Expressions. Adding Unified Expressions to the matching heuristics is an open, unimplemented issue in Resonite's own tracker, and users currently bridge the gap with a third-party mod. Blendshape auto-assignment does opportunistically match VRChat's `vrc.` prefix and some Japanese kana.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Retargeting is the repair when skeletons differ, so its absence costs motion quality rather than the visit.
note: Resonite has no humanoid animation retargeting. Its animation format binds tracks to a node name and a field name, not to a body-part abstraction, so an animation authored for one body does not transfer to another. The documentation goes further and says you cannot drive a VRIK rig with an animation at all — the engine fights it — and recommends posing users with anchors instead.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Equipped items are named in the use case, and attachment points that do not survive leave items on the floor or on the wrong bone.
note: The engine gives you attachment machinery — AvatarObjectSlot and AvatarPoseNode let separate avatar pieces bind to named body nodes, and Snapper handles accessories such as hats and glasses — so items genuinely do travel with a user between worlds inside their inventory. What is missing is an agreed convention for fitting a garment to an unfamiliar body. The wiki's "Avatar standard" page is explicitly a user proposal, with at least one widely used competing fork, and it admits blendshape names are avatar-specific.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Reduced forms matter for crowds and weak devices, and their absence costs frames, not presence.
note: There is no avatar level of detail, no avatar performance ranking, and no built-in avatar culling. Crowd handling is left entirely to user-built systems, and the documentation says plainly that none of them work properly. Resonite's own comparison table for incoming VRChat users lists avatar performance blocking as not applicable.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Without a way to bind an avatar to a verifiable identity, the person who arrives cannot be shown to be the person who left.
note: An avatar can be bound to one cloud user for permission purposes — SimpleAvatarProtection names a single user who may wear, save or export it — but that is asset ownership, not identity. Resonite's docs explicitly warn that what an avatar displays about who you are is not trustworthy: nameplates and badges are avatar-author-controlled and can be faked, and users are told to check the server-side Session screen instead. There is no credential or attestation concept.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Mass and velocity carried across make a moved object behave nearly the same; their absence changes the behaviour without stopping it.
note: The engine ships BepuPhysics2, but rigid bodies are NOT exposed to creators. Resonite's own wiki page for the physics library carries a note on its demonstration video reading that this is what the engine can do, not what is available in Resonite, and points at an open GitHub issue as the tracker for exposing it. What creators actually have is a character controller and collision events. Full rigid-body physics is a named future feature.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Collision shapes travel separately from visible geometry, and losing them means objects pass through each other until the destination builds its own.
note: Eight collider shapes are exposed as components — box, capsule, cone, convex hull, cylinder, mesh, sphere and triangle — each with an offset, a type, a mass and a flag for whether avatars are blocked by it. Collision shapes are authored separately from visible geometry, which is what the capability asks for. There are documented behavioural gaps: active colliders do not raise events against other active colliders, and mesh colliders only collide with primitive colliders.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Hinges and sliders that do not survive turn an assembly into loose parts, which is a loss of behaviour rather than of the asset.
note: No joints or constraints are exposed. There is no wiki page for joints, hinges or constraints, and searches turn up only podcast discussion. This follows from rigid bodies not being exposed — with no dynamic bodies there is nothing to constrain. The nearest thing is dynamic bone chains for wiggle, which is a procedural effect rather than a constraint solver.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Friction and restitution numbers mean different things to different solvers, so agreeing on them buys little and each world may keep its own feel.
note: No physics materials. Colliders expose a mass field and nothing else about surface response; there is no documented friction or restitution anywhere. Again a consequence of rigid bodies not being exposed.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Two engines producing the same trajectory would let one object be simulated in two places at once, and nothing does that today.
note: Resonite makes no determinism claim. The whole networking design removes the need for it: one machine is the host and its data model is replicated to everyone else, so clients do not independently simulate and do not need to agree bit-for-bit.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Cloth and hair are the visible part, so a moved avatar arrives stiff rather than absent.
note: No cloth and no soft-body simulation is documented. Dynamic bone chains provide secondary motion on skeletal chains, which is a different thing and does not solve deformable surfaces.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Regions that fire events are part of how content behaves, and their loss makes the content inert rather than unreadable.
note: Trigger volumes are properly supported and are the main way physics is actually used in Resonite content. Collider types include Trigger, StaticTrigger and haptic trigger variants, and a generalized event system raises contact start, contact stay and contact end. Events are surfaced through relay and listener components that in-world scripting can hook.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Positioned sounds are authored into a scene, and losing them leaves a silent room.
note: Positioned audio sources are a first-class component with the expected controls: volume, spatial blend between 3D and 2D, Doppler level, logarithmic or linear rolloff, minimum and maximum distance, priority, and per-user exclusion. Sources are grouped by type — sound effects, multimedia, voice, user interface — so users can mix categories independently. All of it is Resonite components; nothing exports.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: How direction is turned into sound at the ears is the receiving system's method, like a rendering method.
note: Resonite replaced its old hybrid audio path with Awwdio, an in-house multi-threaded audio system, and spatialization comes from a direct integration of Valve's Steam Audio. An explicit AudioListener component decides where audio is heard from and can double as a virtual microphone, and sources expose a spatialization start distance and transition range. Steam Audio does head-related transfer function rendering, but Resonite's documentation never says the words HRTF or ambisonics, so do not claim either specifically.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A space's acoustic description is authored with it, and without agreement the room sounds wrong rather than silent.
note: Reverb is real and recently reworked: Zita Reverb replaced the legacy reverb zones, it is a stereo effect, and reverb zones now apply to spatialized sources including user voices in normal mode. Sources can opt out with an ignore-reverb-zones flag. It is a reverb-zone model rather than a simulated-acoustics model, and it is authored as Resonite components with no exchange representation.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: The receiving runtime works this out from its own geometry, frame by frame.
note: Sound is not blocked or muffled by geometry. The audio listener's effect chain is documented as carrying reverb zones only, with more described as future work, and there is no occlusion or obstruction component. Steam Audio can do occlusion; Resonite's integration does not document using it.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A visitor can be given audio by other means, so disagreement costs quality and scale.
note: Audio streams ride the same session transport as everything else and are Opus-encoded, and audio files are delivered as ordinary content-addressed assets over HTTPS. There is no separate scalable audio-streaming path — like voice, streamed audio goes to every client through the host, so it does not scale independently of session size.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A visitor who cannot be heard is diminished but still present, and text remains a fallback.
note: Voice is Opus, from a Yellow Dog Man fork of the reference library, with RNNoise for noise suppression. Five modes: Mute, Whisper, Normal, Shout and Broadcast, where Broadcast turns spatialization off entirely. The codec is a real standard; the transport is Resonite's own unencrypted session stream, and voice goes to everyone in the session regardless of mode.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A client or agent that cannot read the destination's state stream arrives blind, which ends both use cases on the spot.
note: This is Resonite's single most distinctive property. Replication is not something a developer opts into per object — the data-model primitives are built so that everything in them replicates and persists automatically, over a binary protocol. Fields marked as "driven" are the documented exception and stay local. It is a genuine full-data-model sync, and it is entirely proprietary: nothing outside Resonite speaks it.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Disagreement about who owns an arriving object shows up as rubber-banding and contested edits rather than as a failed arrival.
note: Authority is coarse and centralised: exactly one host per session, and if the host leaves the session ends. There is no documented host migration. Below that, exclusive write control over an individual element is expressed as "linkage" — a driver takes exclusive control of a field — rather than as transferable per-object ownership. Roles (Admin, Builder, Moderator, Guest, Spectator) govern what a user may do, not who owns what.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Without agreement the destination sends everything or too little, which costs scale.
note: There is no interest management. The design replicates the whole world to everyone, and the documented consequences follow: initial world synchronization time scales with total element count, and voice is sent to every user in the session regardless of whisper range — whisper only changes how far it can be HEARD, not who receives the stream. Video is relayed through the host to all clients.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Latency hiding is local repair work, so its absence is felt as lag.
note: No client-side prediction, reconciliation, rollback or lag compensation is documented anywhere. Wiki searches for those terms return nothing in the article namespace, and none of the architecture, data-model or update pages mention any latency-hiding mechanism. This is an absence of documentation rather than proof of absence in the code.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: With no shared wire protocol there is no session to join at all.
note: Three documented session transports — LiteNetLib over UDP, QUIC (experimental, still missing NAT punch-through), and Steam Sockets — plus a NAT punch-through service and regional relay fallback. All ports are dynamic; port forwarding and UPnP are explicitly unsupported. The transports are ordinary technology but what rides on them is a closed binary protocol, so a third party cannot speak it. Live session traffic is documented as unencrypted by default.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Live audio and video degrade or drop out while the visit continues.
note: Live video sharing exists and is host-relayed over the session's own transport, needing no external server. Ingest is a fixed localhost RTMP endpoint with h264 video and AAC audio and no negotiation — not WebRTC, not SRT. Inbound remote streams accept RTMP and RTSP but not their encrypted variants. Streaming can be disabled per role.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Joining a running world, authentication included, is the door: no agreement, no entry.
note: Session establishment is fully documented and works: six access levels from Private through Anyone, bearer-token authentication with optional TOTP two-factor, and a public unauthenticated listing endpoint. The catch is the compatibility hash — a client can only join if its data-model hash matches the host's exactly, which locks joining to one build of one implementation.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: This row is the portal itself, and the travel use case is nothing but the handoff.
note: You can carry state between worlds, in two ways. Your cloud inventory follows you everywhere. And "transfer grabbing" lets you literally hold an object while changing worlds and arrive with it — but the docs warn that anything referenced in the world's Assets slot is lost because the references break. So objects move; the things they point at do not reliably move with them.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A roster that does not cross operators means you cannot see who is where, but you can still be there.
note: Presence works well inside Resonite: a SignalR connection over WebSocket carries status updates, session updates and contact changes, and contacts are bilateral. It is single-operator. Nothing federates presence across operators, and Universes explicitly hide their users from the main network.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A destination name that does not resolve cannot be travelled to, so naming and resolution are the first agreement.
note: Resonite has a real, documented, human-readable addressing scheme for saved content: `resrec:///[OWNER]/[RECORD_ID]` or `resrec:///[OWNER]/[PATH/TO/RECORD]`. It is registered as an operating-system protocol handler so a link in a browser opens the item in game, and public records resolve over the HTTP API without authentication. It resolves only against Resonite's cloud, so it names places and things inside one operator's namespace.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Worlds can be reached by a known address, so discovery adds reach rather than making it possible.
note: Public session discovery is real and open: `GET /sessions` returns running public sessions and needs no authentication, worlds are searchable through a paged search endpoint, and there is an MIT-licensed official web browser listing every public world and session. Discovery covers Resonite's own cloud only, and Universes deliberately partition it — a Universe's sessions are invisible from the main list and vice versa.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A shared clock keeps events in order; without one the ordering drifts and coarse clocks still hold the session together.
note: There is a synchronized world time available to in-world scripting, exposed through a component that outputs current world time and through ProtoFlux nodes. It is a session-local clock for ordering in-world events, not a cross-operator time standard.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: With no shared base identifier the same person or agent is a stranger in every world they enter.
note: Identity is a Resonite account: an immutable `U-` prefixed user ID, distinct from the display username, plus a per-installation Machine ID derived from an RSA keypair hashed with SHA-256. It is a single-operator identifier with no external resolution. Notably, SAML single sign-on IS available at every tier, so an enterprise can authenticate its own people INTO Resonite — but the resulting identity is still a Resonite record and nothing exports outward.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Claims about age, membership or ownership are worthless if the receiving world cannot read them.
note: There is no verifiable credential format. Authentication is a bespoke bearer token — `Authorization: res <user-id>:<token>` — with a hardware-derived UID header, plus optional TOTP two-factor. Resonite's own two-factor page names FIDO keys, magic links and web3 authentication as things it does NOT support and points people at the issue tracker. No W3C verifiable credential or decentralised identifier concept appears anywhere.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A credential nobody can ask for or present is not a credential, and one subject reaches this row natively today.
note: The only credential-exchange protocols documented are inbound authentication ones: SAML for enterprise sign-in, and an OAuth path that Yellow Dog Man's own sample repository describes as still under construction with credentials handed out manually. Neither is a mechanism for two worlds to request and present claims about a user.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A world that cannot read what an arriving person or agent is allowed to do must either refuse it or trust it blindly.
note: Permission grants exist as world roles — Admin, Builder, Moderator, Guest, Spectator — and are enforced by the session host. They are not readable by any party that did not issue them; they live inside one session's data model. Separately, `resdb:///` links function as unauthenticated bearer capabilities, which is a capability grant of a sort but one that cannot be scoped, audited or revoked.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Without selective disclosure the traveller over-shares, which is a harm rather than a stop.
note: There is no selective disclosure mechanism. Identity is a single account record held by one operator; there is no notion of revealing a subset of claims to a receiving world, because there are no claims and there are no independent receiving worlds.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Relationships and standing that do not travel leave the person present but unknown.
note: A bilateral contacts graph exists and is queryable through the API for your own account, and Yellow Dog Man publishes an account downloader specifically so users can exercise data rights and take a copy out. So the graph is exportable. It is not portable in any operational sense — nothing consumes it elsewhere, and the exporter's stated non-goal is cross-engine compatibility.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: The terms themselves must cross, and that row is a must; acting on them is the receiver's own behaviour, and no agreed mechanism exists yet.
note: There is exactly one enforcement primitive and it is narrow: SimpleAvatarProtection names a single permitted user and blocks everyone else from wearing, saving or exporting that avatar, and it survives into a `.resonitepackage`. Resonite's own documentation says it is not bulletproof. The world read-only flag is explicitly disclaimed as "not a security/permission mechanism". Everything stronger — asset-level protection, hard permissions — is an open issue. The real remedy is a manually reviewed DMCA process.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Content pinned to the Earth must land in the same place in the other system, and a pose that cannot be read puts it somewhere else.
note: A wiki search for GPS, latitude, geospatial and real-world location returned zero hits. Resonite is a virtual sandbox with no Earth-referenced positioning concept.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A frame disagreement is measured in metres or kilometres, not in taste.
note: No geospatial coordinate reference system concept exists. Resonite documents exactly two coordinate spaces, global and local, both relative to the world root.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: An anchor made on one device never leaves it; the sharing case is the next row.
note: No anchoring-to-physical-place concept is documented. Resonite is a fully virtual platform without a passthrough or world-mapping feature set.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Two people in two systems must see the same thing in the same spot, and today one subject reaches this row, through an extension.
note: No shared or persistent physical-space anchors are documented.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Recovering pose from imagery can fall back to satellite position and manual alignment, at worse accuracy.
note: No visual positioning capability is documented. The only camera-derived 3D capability is importing pre-made Gaussian splat scans, which is content import, not localization.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: City-scale data is streamed by tile, and a tileset the receiving client cannot stream has to be converted before it is usable.
note: No tiled terrain or city streaming is documented.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A structured description of an interior makes placement and routing better; without one both are cruder, and nothing reaches this row today.
note: No structured indoor-space description is documented. ---

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: The visitor's app and the device runtime are two independent systems, and if they cannot start an immersive session the visit does not happen.
note: Resonite does NOT run on OpenXR. It targets SteamVR/OpenVR plus vendor runtimes, selected with command-line device flags, and OpenXR support is explicitly named by the lead developer as something the Unity renderer replacement will unlock in future. This is the single most consequential input finding for a standards study: any assumption that Resonite is OpenXR-conformant today is wrong. There is also no standalone headset client — Quest works only tethered to a PC.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A world that reads controllers differently is harder to use, and pointer and text paths remain.
note: Controller input works through SteamVR and vendor runtimes and is selectable with launch flags for SteamVR, Windows Mixed Reality, Oculus Rift and Oculus Quest, with a legacy SteamVR input path also available. Gamepad support exists but is documented as preliminary — movement, turning, jumping and the context menu. Since the binding goes through SteamVR rather than OpenXR, controller profiles are inherited from Valve's ecosystem rather than from a cross-vendor standard.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Hand tracking adds a way in, and its absence falls back to controllers.
note: Finger tracking is received and displayed — from Leap Motion and from Index controllers — but it is display only. Resonite states plainly that there is no official way to move or interact using hand tracking alone. So hands are an expressive channel, not an input source in the sense the capability describes.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Gaze is an aid with privacy limits, and everything works without it.
note: Eye tracking is a strong, first-class feature rather than a bolt-on. The EyeManager component is set up automatically for avatars with detectable eyes and exposes a detailed per-eye model — openness, widen, squeeze, frown, brow verticals, and pupil size in millimetres — plus simulated saccades when no hardware is present. Several trackers are natively integrated. The data model is Resonite's own; the only external piece is OSC used as a transport for Steam Link data.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Touch feedback is felt when it is missing, and nothing stops.
note: There is a real haptics system with authored haptic volumes, stacking multiplicative filters, and a sampler abstraction so world content can drive feedback. Devices reach it two ways: directly for VR controllers, or over OSC and WebSocket for vests and other hardware. The OSC path is the genuinely open part. The wiki's own status notes are candid that several device integrations are broken or recently repaired.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A world that cannot ask what the arriving device can do will guess, and guessing wrong costs quality rather than entry.
note: The engine does track per-user device capability — logs show finger, eye and lip tracking flags carried against each user — and world content can react to what a user's hardware can do. There is no documented capability-description format and no negotiation protocol; it is an internal flag set surfaced in logs, not something another system can query or that a standard could bind to.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: The language a world writes its rules in is its own business and never has to cross.
note: In-world programming is ProtoFlux only. There is also a documented C# plugin path loaded with a `-LoadAssembly` command-line argument, but the docs are blunt that a plugin touching the data model makes your session unjoinable for anyone without the identical plugin, and there is no distribution system. So plugins are a local extension mechanism, not a portable scripting runtime.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: The use case says the asset must behave, so a door that will not open in the second system is the failure this row names.
note: This is the capability Resonite scores best on in spirit and worst on in portability. ProtoFlux is a node-based visual language that is part of the object: when you export an item as a `.resonitepackage`, the ProtoFlux goes with it, alongside the hierarchy, components and bones. Behaviour genuinely travels with the asset. But it travels only to another Resonite. ProtoFlux runs on a proprietary stack-based virtual machine inside closed-source FrooxEngine, there is no specification, no serialization format anyone else can read, and no standalone runtime. Roughly 1,089 node pages are publicly documented on the wiki, which is a real reference, but a reference is not a spec.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A host can sandbox guest content on its own; agreement only makes the limits predictable for the guest.
note: There is no engine-level sandbox with limits. What exists is a per-world role permission system expressed as components in the world graph — Admin, Builder, Moderator, Guest, Spectator, each inheriting the one below, governing saving, spawning, transferring objects out, avatar swapping and streaming. Above that sits one coarse gate, "Unsafe Mode", which a world must opt into before experimental nodes such as writing files to disk will run, and which can be restricted by a startup-config allowlist. Below it there is nothing: no memory cap, no CPU quota, no execution timeout for guest ProtoFlux, and an impulse chain that does not yield will stall the whole engine. The documented advice for protecting content is social — do not give strangers Builder rights. Note also that Resonite's own security policy does not treat your IP address as private, because sessions are peer to peer.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: An agent with no agreed way to perceive and act in a world it did not come from cannot join it at all.
note: There is no autonomous-agent concept in the engine, but there are two documented doors an external program can drive a world through: ResoniteLink, an MIT-licensed WebSocket and JSON protocol built for exactly this, and C# plugins. Yellow Dog Man name external scripts controlling a live event as a use case. ResoniteLink is explicitly not for real-time control — reads and writes happen "eventually" — and it requires you to be the session host.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Without agreed limits, guest content and agents are throttled or refused unpredictably.
note: There is no enforced resource budget for guest content. All the substantial documentation is advisory optimisation guidance — what makes worlds slow and how to profile it — with no engine-side cap on memory, node count, polygon count or CPU time. The only hard numeric limits documented anywhere are administrative rather than runtime: cloud storage starting at one gigabyte, 256 cloud-variable definitions per user and 8192 per group, a default of 64 audio voices, and a 128-triangle cap on custom 3D badges. Nothing bounds an imported avatar or a spawned item.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: What survives a restart is mostly the host's business; it crosses the boundary only when a visitor's changes must last.
note: Persistence is explicit, not automatic. Nothing survives a session unless someone saves it, and a session ends the moment its host leaves. Autosave exists but is off by default on headless servers. Individual slots carry a `Persistent` boolean, and turning it off excludes that slot and everything under it from the save. The persistence serialization is a deliberately different mode from the network protocol and is built for forwards and backwards compatibility.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: The use case names inventory, and items that cannot be read at the destination do not travel with the person.
note: This is one of the few real cross-world inventory implementations in the study. Every user gets a cloud-backed, folder-structured inventory that follows them to any machine after login, and items spawn into any world. Items CAN leave the platform, as `.resonitepackage` archives — but only back into Resonite. Sharing is by public folder, which works as a capability handed out by link rather than a listing, and content in a shared folder counts only against the owner's quota. Free accounts start with one gigabyte.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: The use case names preferences, and for a person who depends on comfort and accessibility settings, arriving without them ends the visit.
note: Some settings do follow the user rather than the machine — full-body-tracking calibration is documented as tied to the account. There is a full account data export tool published by Yellow Dog Man, so preferences and content can be pulled out. But nothing is portable to another platform: the export tool's README names cross-engine compatibility as an explicit non-goal.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Naming content by hash makes an item the same item everywhere; without it copies drift while still loading.
note: This is a real, shipped content-addressing implementation, not a design intention. Every asset is named by the SHA-256 hash of its own bytes, referenced as `resdb:///<hash>.<ext>`, de-duplicated on upload and against the user's storage quota, and fetchable over plain HTTPS at `assets.resonite.com/<hash>`. Two caveats matter: the links are unauthenticated, so possession of a hash is possession of the content; and Resonite's own release notes advise creators to prefer `resrec:///` because `resdb:///` links are not guaranteed.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A runnable experience moves between hosts far less often than an asset does, and repackaging is the fallback.
note: `.resonitepackage` is a documented ZIP bundle carrying record metadata plus a SHA256-named asset store, and it does package a complete runnable thing — hierarchy, components, ProtoFlux, all assets. But it is only runnable inside Resonite. The docs list offline editing and third-party export as explicit non-goals.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Assets reach clients over ordinary web delivery, so agreement here buys scale and cost rather than possibility.
note: Three documented delivery paths: ordinary HTTP(S)/FTP URLs fetched by each client directly; Resonite's own hash-addressed asset store at `assets.resonite.com`; and `local://` assets that never touch the cloud and move inside the session between participants. Saving to the cloud rewrites `local://` references to `resdb://`.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A reader that cannot tell which version it holds, or what to do with the parts it does not know, breaks on the first update, which is the "no hand fixes" test again.
note: Long-term compatibility of saved content is a stated engine commitment, and there is machinery behind it: the open-source Elements.Data library exists partly to handle type upgrades, carrying attributes for old type names, old namespaces, old assemblies and type replacement. The stated flip side is that content built on unimplemented hacks or on bug behaviour is not covered.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Every other must row is a claim until a shared test says it holds, which is exactly what the meeting asked for.
note: There is no specification to conform to and no conformance suite. The only published JSON schemas are for headless-server and client configuration files, not for the data model or any wire format, and they are generated from Resonite's source rather than being an independent spec.

subject: Resonite
capability: World generation from a prompt or an image
interop_reason: A generated place that arrives only as frames to watch still reaches the viewer, but as a recording rather than a world the receiver can open and use.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and making a whole three-dimensional place from a description or a picture is not an act it performs or specifies.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A world continued by a model still reaches a viewer, but only as what the model chooses to show, so the receiver cannot keep it or run it again.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and it never continues a world under a viewer's actions from a learned model; there is no such model here.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: How a system turns photographs into a model is its own method, and what leaves is an ordinary asset the container and geometry rows already carry.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and turning a set of ordinary photographs into a textured three-dimensional model is not among its jobs.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so this row is what geometry encoding is for a mesh: splat content in a named format the receiving tool cannot read does not arrive at all, and re-exporting it is the hand fix the use case forbids.
note: This is the one genuinely round-trippable open capture path on the whole map. Both the plain PLY form and Niantic's SPZ are read and written, and a PLY can be recompressed to SPZ on import. Radiance fields other than Gaussian splatting are not documented, so do not read a wider claim into it.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Without an agreed order for what arrives first, a large capture still loads, it just makes the viewer wait for the whole of it.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and it delivers no captured scene, progressively by region and detail or otherwise.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a volumetric clip is an asset like any other: without the calibration and mask metadata a second implementation needs, what arrives is not the recording and no one can make it one by hand.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and it carries no captured, time-varying three-dimensional scene as media, and no camera calibration or mask metadata for one.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a point cloud encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a point cloud, exactly as an undecodable mesh is not a mesh, and that capture shows nothing.
note: Point clouds come in from the lidar interchange formats and from an ASCII form, and internally become the same mesh class with a point topology rather than triangles. The direction is one way: no point cloud export is documented at any format, so scanned data goes in and cannot come back out.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so views that arrive without their intrinsics and extrinsics cannot be reprojected: the capture lands as loose pictures rather than as the place it recorded.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and it carries no set of calibrated camera views with per-pixel depth, and no intrinsics or extrinsics to reproject them.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Making an image from a viewpoint no camera occupied is a method inside one system, and what crosses to a second system is the picture it produced.
note: Drawing an imported capture from any viewpoint is what the splat asset does, and the platform ships the renderer for it rather than pointing at someone else's.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a moving capture handed over as unrelated frames is not the capture: the receiver has to guess the rate and the ordering the sender already knew, and guessing is the hand fix the use case forbids.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and it carries no captured scene that changes over time, and states no rate at which one should be played back.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Whether a captured scene answers the light around it is work the receiving system does, and the asset arrives either way.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and it holds no captured scene that could be made to answer the light of the place it lands in.

subject: Resonite
capability: Editing a capture after the fact
interop_reason: Editing a capture happens in the tool that holds it, and what leaves is the edited asset, which the format rows already carry.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and there is no capture here to crop, delete from or recolour, and no export for such an edit to survive.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Describing a change to a world you already made is one service's own interface, and the world that results still leaves by the ordinary export rows.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and there is no generated world here to change by describing the change or pointing at a region.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A generator that cannot read the specification another tool wrote still produces a world, it just will not be the world that was asked for.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and nothing here accepts a specification of a world that should be made.

subject: Resonite
capability: Deriving conventional assets from a generated scene
interop_reason: Derived meshes and panoramas are how a generated world reaches a conventional engine at all, and each route loses something the receiver has to be told about.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and it derives no collision mesh, drawing mesh, panorama or video from a splat or radiance-field world.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Actions that arrive without their embodiment, frame and units cannot be replayed elsewhere, so an agent acts only in the system it was written for.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and it carries no agent's actions in or out as time-sampled data with an embodiment, a frame and units.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A panorama whose projection is not stated is still an image, but the receiver has to guess before it can use it as a backdrop or as a light.
note: Resonite is a platform whose import and export paths are unusually open for a hosted world, and it carries no full 360-degree view of a place as an image with its projection stated.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A reconstruction that cannot leave the device that made it keeps the room private to one session, so anything placed against it has to be fitted again elsewhere.
note: A fully virtual social platform whose base coordinate space is its own world root and cannot be changed. Sessions hold authored and imported content; there is no reading of the physical room around a headset.

subject: Resonite
capability: Semantic labelling of the real world
interop_reason: Labels each vendor names differently still serve one application, but a second one cannot act on floor or sky without being rewritten for that vendor.
note: Its labels describe its own data model — slots, components and assets — not real surfaces. Nothing classifies a floor or a wall that a camera can see.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Depth reported in units the receiver does not share puts real surfaces at the wrong distance, so content is placed badly rather than not at all.
note: No depth of the physical world enters the platform. Depth in Resonite is the depth of its own rendered scene, which is a different thing from a measurement of the room.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Whether real surfaces hide virtual content is drawn on the device that sees them, and none of that decision crosses to a second system.
note: Content is composited against the virtual world only. Without a passthrough view or real-world depth, hiding virtual objects behind real ones does not arise.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: How much of the real room a runtime lets through is its own presentation, and an arriving asset cannot tell the difference.
note: Resonite's published feature list is about headsets, tracking systems and platforms it runs on; no component or world setting mixes a live camera view of the room into the render, and the wiki's uses of the word passthrough are about interaction and teleport targets. Read off the feature and component documentation rather than stated by the project, so recorded unverified.

subject: Resonite
capability: Face and body tracking as input
interop_reason: A face and body stream in a shape the receiver does not read leaves the avatar still rather than absent, and its privacy terms have to be agreed with it.
note: Among the strongest on this row. Resonite supports a range of face and eye tracking systems through native integration as well as plug-ins and mods, and the eye model it exposes is detailed enough to include pupil size, which is a genuine live sensor stream of the person rather than a stored expression. The privacy terms are the platform's own, and a session's participants see the result on the avatar.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A place that arrives without its walkable surface and arrival points still loads, but whoever opens it has to work out where a body may stand and where a portal lands.
note: Arrival is declared and the floor is not. A component in the world creation set spawns a user where the author wants them, so a world says where a visitor appears; nothing declares walkable surface or bounds, and a body's movement is decided by the physics of whatever geometry is there.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A published unit of logic whose name resolves to something else elsewhere still runs, but nobody can be sure which code they called.
note: Every item is a record with its own durable address, and those addresses are registered with the operating system so a link spawns the item in the session — a real permanent name for a published thing, including one that carries logic. It is ownership by account and folder rather than a namespace: names are not reserved to an author across the platform, and nothing guarantees the record behind an address is unchanged.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A receiving world that cannot tell what review arriving content has already had still shows it, and has to repeat the whole review itself.
note: Review happens after publication and by hand: the Resonite team reviews copyright claims manually, and nothing stands between an item leaving a creator's folder and another person spawning it. A receiving session learns nothing about what review an arriving item has had.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Two maps of one place with no published transform between them put the same content in two positions, so a person arrives beside where they meant to be.
note: Resonite worlds are virtual. There is no map of a real place, so nothing to version or align.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A service that never declares where it applies still answers, so a client has to call it and find out instead of testing whether it is relevant.
note: No world or service in Resonite declares a region of the Earth where it applies.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A receiver must distinguish required additions from optional ones or it cannot safely interpret an arriving asset or exchange.
note: The plugin system declares runtime assemblies and warns that data-model changes require participants to have the same plugins to join.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Content still arrives when color conventions differ, but its colors and brightness can change visibly.
note: ColorX carries color-profile metadata and provides profile conversion nodes; this type page does not establish the complete rendering-surface output-range contract.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A moved asset remains usable without a shared preview image, but selection and arrival previews become slower or less informative.
note: WorldTextureThumbnailSource attaches a chosen image texture to a world as its thumbnail, avoiding the need for the recipient to render the world for a preview.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A scene or visit can continue when interface layouts differ, but carried controls and information may become hard to use.
note: UIX defines canvases, fractional anchors and automatic layouts for interfaces.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: An asset with external resources cannot load intact if the receiver cannot resolve its resource references in the intended context.
note: Assets have URI references and explicit loading behavior; this overview does not specify all context-dependent scheme-resolution rules.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Turning local pointing input into a scene hit stays inside the receiving application and does not require agreement between independent worlds.
note: GetRawDataToolHit reports raycast hits from a user's tool.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Receiving text through a local input field or keyboard interface is a device-side interaction and need not be shared between worlds.
note: The UIX TextField component receives text entry and exposes user interaction through ProtoFlux UI nodes.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Shared bounds let a receiver select content before loading its geometry; without them the content can still move but loads and traverses less efficiently.
note: The official slot-performance documentation describes computing a slot bounding box for gizmos; it does not establish pre-load rejection or spatial indexing.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A moved object or avatar can still load when constraints are lost, but linked movement and pose behavior degrade.
note: CopyGlobalTransform drives an object's global position and rotation from another slot, with source fields, update order and pre-physics evaluation documented.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A scene can transfer without agreed media timing, but its video, sound and coordinated presentation can be lost or drift.
note: ProtoFlux exposes playable media controls and SyncPlayback position or speed driving for scene playback.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A recipient that cannot interpret the carried permission cannot determine whether the requested use of the subject or data is authorized.
note: The early OAuth service requires user consent and named profile/email/offline scopes, but this page does not define complete grant-purpose, expiry and withdrawal records; registration needs manual approval.

subject: Resonite
capability: Deciding whether to admit an arrival
interop_reason: A traveller or agent cannot safely complete entry unless the origin and destination understand the destination's approval, refusal and validity conditions.
note: Join Verify provides allow and deny responses before a user joins; the captured category does not settle response validity limits or a portable response format.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: An asset can still load with fallback materials when its shaders are not understood, but authored appearance degrades.
note: The official wiki explicitly excludes custom shader programs, including Unity shaders; a future node-based shader plan does not supply a current portable shader language.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: A receiver that cannot evaluate the transmitted curves and surfaces cannot reconstruct an asset whose geometry is carried in that form.
note: BezierCurve stores controlling curve points and coordinate space and drives a synchronized curve used by BezierTubeMesh; the component can be saved with scene content.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Losing an exchanged emitter's parameters removes or changes visual effects while the containing asset or avatar can still arrive.
note: The saved ParticleSystem component references emitters and ParticleStyle, with maximum particle count and simulation coordinate space defined.

subject: Resonite
interop_reason: Without an agreed musical-event interface, an arriving performance or interactive experience loses instrument input while other interaction paths remain.
note: The official OSC guide names the ofxOscMidi bridge for receiving instrument MIDI as OSC; the captured integration description does not define the resulting typed channel, note and control interface.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: How a system turns geometry into pixels never leaves that system, so two runtimes can draw the same scene by different means and nothing crosses.
note: Roblox has a full rasteriser but publishes nothing about its render graph or pass structure, and creators cannot author passes or shaders. The only creator-facing view of pass structure is a read-only debug tool that reports counts per pass. A search of the whole documentation set finds no mention of custom shaders or shader code.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: The graphics interface a runtime targets is a build choice inside one system, and an arriving asset cannot tell the difference.
note: The engine targets four low-level graphics interfaces and picks one automatically per device. This is an engine setting, not a creator binding — there is no way to supply your own graphics code.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: An asset that arrives against a different surface model still loads, but the further apart the two models are the more the look drifts.
note: Surfaces are described by a physically-based material with colour, normal, roughness, metalness and emissive maps, plus a library of built-in materials and creator-defined variants. One constraint that bites on import: only one material per mesh object, and normal maps must be in one specific convention.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: A moved scene whose lights are read differently is lit wrong rather than lost.
note: Several named lighting systems exist, from a coarse voxel light map through shadow mapping to the highest-fidelity option, plus point, spot and surface lights and an ambient term derived from the sky. The choice of system is a property value; the algorithms are not published.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: Effects applied after the main pass are the receiving system's taste and carry nothing across.
note: A fixed set of post effects is offered as objects a creator drops into the scene: bloom, blur, colour correction, colour grading, depth of field and sun rays. Creators pick from the set; they cannot write their own effect.

subject: Roblox
capability: Level of detail and streaming order
interop_reason: Without an agreed order for what to send first, a large scene still arrives, it just pops and stalls on the way in.
note: Three layers of detail control exist: an automatic per-mesh fidelity that steps down with camera distance, a cloud-built simplified stand-in system for whole models and avatars, and a radius-based streaming system that decides what to send first. The simplified stand-ins are generated on Roblox servers, so the mechanism cannot be used outside Roblox.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: Only content captured as splats is affected: a system that cannot draw them shows nothing of it, while mesh content is untouched.
note: A text search of the whole published documentation set finds no mention of Gaussian splatting or radiance fields. The only hits for "Gaussian" are the blur post effect.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: The same holds for point clouds and volumetric video, which travel in forms few systems read.
note: Terrain is a real voxel system with a scripting interface to read and write voxels, but the grid size is fixed and cannot be changed. There is nothing for point clouds or volumetric video — those words do not appear in the documentation at all.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: Labels, signs and name tags lose their font and layout when the two systems disagree, so the text degrades while the rest of the asset is fine.
note: Text is drawn into the 3D world by attaching a flat interface surface to a part face, or a camera-facing panel in space. Fonts are ordinary Roblox assets with a family, weight and style.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: Authored viewpoints are part of a scene, and losing them costs the arrival shot, not the scene.
note: There is a built-in camera object with third-person and first-person modes, replaceable by creator code, and a headset variant that reports device pose as a position-and-orientation value. Viewpoints are named by Roblox object references, not by any portable camera description.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: If the receiving system cannot rebuild the same tree, parenting and transforms collapse and the asset does not assemble at all.
note: Everything in a place is one tree of objects, called the data model, and that tree is the engine's source of truth. The tree only exists inside Roblox; nothing else can read it.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: A disagreement about handedness or axis order puts every object in the wrong place or mirrored, which is the classic hand fix.
note: The axis convention is friendly — right-handed, Y up, forward along negative Z, the same convention glTF uses, and the documented import setting for modelling tools is Y up. The gap is that Roblox's transform value carries only position and a 3x3 rotation, with no scale component; object size lives in a separate property. A scaled node from another tool therefore cannot round-trip through a Roblox transform.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: The file is the boundary: if the second system cannot open it, nothing else on this list matters.
note: Roblox's own container files are `.rbxl` and `.rbxlx` for places and `.rbxm` and `.rbxmx` for models. The binary variants are described only as "compact, but not human-readable" — no byte-level specification is published anywhere by Roblox — and the upload documentation warns outright that files touched by anything other than Roblox Studio may not work. This is a closed container that cannot be a neutral interchange format for anyone.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: A mesh encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a mesh, and the compression choice is where this usually breaks.
note: Roblox READS `.fbx`, `.obj` and `.gltf` and applies hard limits (20,000 triangles per mesh, watertight, no n-gons, at most four bone influences per vertex). It can WRITE geometry back out as glTF, but that is a beta feature, and separately as a plain `.obj` through a legacy plugin call. The internal encoding and compression of a stored Roblox mesh is not published at all.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: Device-specific texture compression is the common failure: the model arrives untextured and someone must re-export it.
note: Images go in as `.png`, `.jpg`, `.tga` or `.bmp`; textures are capped at 4096 by 4096 and the engine re-encodes and streams its own quality levels. No compressed device texture format is exposed to creators either on the way in or on the way out — there is no mention anywhere in the documentation of the usual transmission or GPU texture container formats.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: Carrying materials without loss is what "renders in another system" means, and only two subjects reach this row natively today.
note: There is no material interchange. A search of the whole documentation set finds no mention of MaterialX or Universal Scene Description. Roblox's surface-appearance object is its own thing; the beta glTF export carries texture images but not a portable material graph.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: A clip that cannot be read leaves the object still, and an avatar that cannot move is not an avatar.
note: This is a clean read-only asymmetry. Animation comes IN on an `.fbx` or `.gltf` (one clip per file) and becomes a Roblox asset referenced by a numeric ID; the beta glTF exporter explicitly cannot write animation back out. Animation authored in Roblox cannot leave Roblox.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: The bone hierarchy is what makes a body move correctly elsewhere; without an agreed one, motion has nothing to bind to.
note: Roblox publishes the exact bone names and parent-child order that a humanoid rig must use, plus a higher-fidelity variant adding up to 37 optional bones for hands, shoulders and spine. This is one of the more genuinely reusable things Roblox has published, because the names are stated in the open documentation.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: Blend shapes carry facial detail, so losing them freezes a face rather than stopping the transfer.
note: Shape deformation is documented only for animatable avatar heads, where it is expressed as a named set of facial poses stored as blend shapes in the source model. There is no documented general morph-target support for ordinary meshes.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: A scene without agreed instancing still loads, it just costs far more memory and frames.
note: The engine collapses repeated identical meshes into one draw call automatically; the creator's job is only to reuse the same mesh and texture rather than to declare instances. There is no explicit instancing object or API, and no instancing information survives into any file Roblox can write. (Careful: the word "Instance" in the Roblox API means "an object in the data model" and has nothing to do with this.)

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: Layered references are a working convenience, and flattening on export is the fallback that keeps the asset moving.
note: Packages give real referencing, nesting, automatic update and version history, and a copy of a package can override the root attribute values it was published with — those overrides survive an update while everything else is refreshed. The override granularity is limited to those root attributes, and the whole mechanism is Studio-authoring-time and Roblox-only.

subject: Roblox
interop_reason: A metre read as a centimetre makes the asset useless on arrival, and rescaling by hand is the fix the use case forbids.
note: This is a hard collision with any metre-based common approach. Roblox's length unit, the stud, is officially 28 centimetres, not a metre. Its mass unit is 21.952 kilograms. Its default gravity is 196.2 studs per second squared, which the same page states is 54.936 metres per second squared — about five and a half times Earth gravity — and Roblox lists 35 studs per second squared as the separate "realistic" value. Content moved either way needs a 0.28 scale factor and a gravity change, and Roblox states the engine itself does no unit conversion at all.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: The use case names preferences, and for a person who depends on comfort and accessibility settings, arriving without them ends the visit.
note: Storage is keyed by the signing organisation, so nothing a user sets travels with them to another publisher's fabric. There is no user-preference or accessibility model in the engine.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Naming content by hash makes an item the same item everywhere; without it copies drift while still loading.
note: Any fetched file may carry an integrity hash in the familiar `algorithm-digest` form over SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512, and modules declare theirs in the manifest, which is real content addressing. The hole is a fail-open in two places at once: the manifest hash field is optional and the published tutorial fabric omits it, and the verifier starts from a true result and only replaces it when a hash is actually present.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: A runnable experience moves between hosts far less often than an asset does, and repackaging is the fallback.
note: One signed file is the runnable package: it carries the container name, the declared services, the module list with optional hashes, the scene data and the presentation block, and the browser signs and verifies it from the command line. Module and asset addresses inside it resolve relative to the fabric's own address, so a fabric plus its files can be dropped on any web server.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Assets reach clients over ordinary web delivery, so agreement here buys scale and cost rather than possibility.
note: Content delivery is plain HTTPS plus a good client-side cache: assets are deduplicated engine-wide by address so two tabs never fetch or write the same file twice, kept on disk across restarts, and invalidated by a single stale timestamp per primary container held in one file. There is no server-side delivery story, no manifest of mirrors and no negotiated tiering. The release channel and installer manifest that do exist deliver the browser itself, not content.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: A reader that cannot tell which version it holds, or what to do with the parts it does not know, breaks on the first update, which is the "no hand fixes" test again.
note: The fabric format carries no version field. The ABI's version constant covers the packet framing only and is explicitly not bumped when methods are added. The consequences are already live and the vendor says so: the release notes tell authors that fabrics made before this release must be updated and that the format will not be stable until version 1.0.0. The drift is visible in the shipped corpus — the engine's own note says the services block is a name-keyed object and every accessor tests for one, while the published tutorial fabrics ship an empty array, which the engine reads as no services and reports no error. The module interface is the opposite story and deserves the credit: method numbers are permanent, monotonic and append-only, superseded methods stay in the header so already-deployed modules keep running, and the version constant is documented as covering the packet framing alone. This subject therefore has an exemplary update rule for its code interface and none at all for its content format. The SDK quotes are from the `prep` branch, identical there to `main`.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Every other must row is a claim until a shared test says it holds, which is exactly what the meeting asked for.
note: There is no specification of the fabric format, no interface document beyond the ABI header, and no conformance suite. The test executable covers engine subsystems — signing, storage, cache, shader validation, compute, the clock — which proves the implementation works, not that a second implementation would agree with it. The cost of having no suite is already visible inside the SDK itself. The reference for the C binding documents the fabric's services as an indexed list read out of the open snapshot, with a count and per-index name, type and endpoint getters; every other page, and the header, say services are keyed by name, served on demand, and deliberately kept out of the snapshot. So two bindings of one interface describe the same block two incompatible ways. Separately, the C reference and the new quickstart both teach the scene method numbers the header marks deprecated. Nothing tests for either. Until a format document and a suite exist, compatible with this browser has no testable meaning. The SDK quotes are from the `prep` branch, identical there to `main`.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
capability: World generation from a prompt or an image
interop_reason: A generated place that arrives only as frames to watch still reaches the viewer, but as a recording rather than a world the receiver can open and use.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and making a whole three-dimensional place from a description or a picture is not an act it performs or specifies.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: A world continued by a model still reaches a viewer, but only as what the model chooses to show, so the receiver cannot keep it or run it again.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and it never continues a world under a viewer's actions from a learned model; there is no such model here.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: How a system turns photographs into a model is its own method, and what leaves is an ordinary asset the container and geometry rows already carry.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and turning a set of ordinary photographs into a textured three-dimensional model is not among its jobs.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so this row is what geometry encoding is for a mesh: splat content in a named format the receiving tool cannot read does not arrive at all, and re-exporting it is the hand fix the use case forbids.
note: The browser sniffs a fetched resource and parses glTF; nothing in the engine reads a splat container, and the glTF path flattens the default scene into meshes, materials and textures rather than handling point primitives with splat attributes.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser

note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and it delivers no captured scene, progressively by region and detail or otherwise.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a volumetric clip is an asset like any other: without the calibration and mask metadata a second implementation needs, what arrives is not the recording and no one can make it one by hand.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and it carries no captured, time-varying three-dimensional scene as media, and no camera calibration or mask metadata for one.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a point cloud encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a point cloud, exactly as an undecodable mesh is not a mesh, and that capture shows nothing.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and it defines no encoding or compression for a set of points with attributes.
