note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and it carries no set of calibrated camera views with per-pixel depth, and no intrinsics or extrinsics to reproject them.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Making an image from a viewpoint no camera occupied is a method inside one system, and what crosses to a second system is the picture it produced.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and it produces no image from a viewing position that no capture camera occupied.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a moving capture handed over as unrelated frames is not the capture: the receiver has to guess the rate and the ordering the sender already knew, and guessing is the hand fix the use case forbids.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and it carries no captured scene that changes over time, and states no rate at which one should be played back.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Whether a captured scene answers the light around it is work the receiving system does, and the asset arrives either way.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and it holds no captured scene that could be made to answer the light of the place it lands in.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
capability: Editing a capture after the fact
interop_reason: Editing a capture happens in the tool that holds it, and what leaves is the edited asset, which the format rows already carry.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and there is no capture here to crop, delete from or recolour, and no export for such an edit to survive.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Describing a change to a world you already made is one service's own interface, and the world that results still leaves by the ordinary export rows.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and there is no generated world here to change by describing the change or pointing at a region.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: A generator that cannot read the specification another tool wrote still produces a world, it just will not be the world that was asked for.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and nothing here accepts a specification of a world that should be made.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
capability: Deriving conventional assets from a generated scene
interop_reason: Derived meshes and panoramas are how a generated world reaches a conventional engine at all, and each route loses something the receiver has to be told about.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and it derives no collision mesh, drawing mesh, panorama or video from a splat or radiance-field world.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Actions that arrive without their embodiment, frame and units cannot be replayed elsewhere, so an agent acts only in the system it was written for.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and it carries no agent's actions in or out as time-sampled data with an embodiment, a frame and units.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: A panorama whose projection is not stated is still an image, but the receiver has to guess before it can use it as a backdrop or as a light.
note: The Open Metaverse Browser is a client that opens a spatial fabric file and fetches whatever the file points at, and it carries no full 360-degree view of a place as an image with its projection stated.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: A reconstruction that cannot leave the device that made it keeps the room private to one session, so anything placed against it has to be fitted again elsewhere.
note: The browser architecture names scene understanding among the capabilities it expects, and hands every one of them to OpenXR extensions rather than defining anything itself. So a reconstruction of the room may reach an application through the runtime underneath, but this project's own specification carries no room geometry, no format for it and no way to pass it on.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
capability: Semantic labelling of the real world
interop_reason: Labels each vendor names differently still serve one application, but a second one cannot act on floor or sky without being rewritten for that vendor.
note: Semantic labelling of real surfaces is inside the same deferral: it belongs to the scene understanding the architecture leaves to OpenXR. Nothing in the project's own interfaces names a real floor, wall or object.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Depth reported in units the receiver does not share puts real surfaces at the wrong distance, so content is placed badly rather than not at all.
note: No depth of the real world is defined. The architecture treats the raw camera feed of the user's surroundings as data of extreme sensitivity to be kept away from content, and defines no depth channel of its own.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Whether real surfaces hide virtual content is drawn on the device that sees them, and none of that decision crosses to a second system.
note: Passthrough is listed as an OpenXR extension the browser expects to sit under it, not as something the browser specifies. There is no rule here for how a real surface hides virtual content.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: How much of the real room a runtime lets through is its own presentation, and an arriving asset cannot tell the difference.
note: The browser's preview target is a flat or headset display of the fabric it opens. Nothing in its architecture notes mixes a camera view of the room into that picture.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
capability: Face and body tracking as input
interop_reason: A face and body stream in a shape the receiver does not read leaves the avatar still rather than absent, and its privacy terms have to be agreed with it.
note: The browser passes device input to modules. There is no face or body sensing surface in its published interface for a module to read.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: A place that arrives without its walkable surface and arrival points still loads, but whoever opens it has to work out where a body may stand and where a portal lands.
note: The browser walks a fabric of nodes and attachment points and works out its own view of the scene. No node type declares walkable surface, bounds or an arrival point, so where a person stands when a fabric opens is the browser's guess rather than the author's statement.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: A published unit of logic whose name resolves to something else elsewhere still runs, but nobody can be sure which code they called.
note: Modules are addressed by a name and an endpoint inside one manifest, and the browser loads what that endpoint serves. There is no registry making the name permanent and nothing preventing another author from using it.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: A receiving world that cannot tell what review arriving content has already had still shows it, and has to repeat the whole review itself.
note: The browser verifies the signature and the chain on a manifest before parsing it, which establishes who published the content and not what review it has had. Nothing arriving tells the browser whether anybody has looked at the content, and the browser performs no review of its own.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Two maps of one place with no published transform between them put the same content in two positions, so a person arrives beside where they meant to be.
note: The browser has no geographic model: content is fetched by address, not placed on Earth, so there is no map to declare or align.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: A service that never declares where it applies still answers, so a client has to call it and find out instead of testing whether it is relevant.
note: Discovery is by address, so a client never asks what is relevant where it is standing and nothing published for the browser declares an area of application.

note: The SDK exposes author-defined service JSON as text; the service vocabulary and property types are not fixed by that interface.

note: The separately scoped Sneeze SDK/MSF documentation carries certificate identity, key fingerprint and signature/trust-chain evaluation evidence with fabric claims. This is that SDK/module route; it is not asserted as implemented by the pinned Forum engine.

interop_reason: A scene or visit can continue when interface layouts differ, but carried controls and information may become hard to use.
note: The Forum engine's RmlUi integration rasterizes UI panels for scene surfaces; this is an engine dependency, not portable guest UI behavior.

interop_reason: An asset with external resources cannot load intact if the receiver cannot resolve its resource references in the intended context.
note: The separately scoped Sneeze SDK resolves document identifiers against the fabric or an absolute URL and fetches the resource. This is the named SDK route, without attributing the vendor API to the pinned Forum engine.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Shared bounds let a receiver select content before loading its geometry; without them the content can still move but loads and traverses less efficiently.
note: MapObject carries three bounding dimensions; the cited setter does not define a pre-load spatial index or traversal behavior.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Without agreed links and transform meaning, receivers cannot reconstruct the same related frames for transferred content or participants.
note: The pinned Forum Sneeze glTF loader reads scene nodes with local transforms and child indices from glTF/GLB and composes children under their parent transform.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
capability: Record of what a system decided
interop_reason: A shared evaluation receipt makes cross-system actions auditable, while travel or participation can still occur without that record.
note: The separate Sneeze SDK/MSF module exposes machine-readable signature and certificate trust results. The retained passage does not define an acceptance/rejection/action receipt from a relying recipient.

subject: Open Metaverse Browser
interop_reason: Choosing and dispatching internal GPU computation does not require agreement between the systems that exchange an asset.
note: The pinned Forum engine compute module dispatches SPIR-V kernels through Vox; guest SDK exposure is not established.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: How a system turns geometry into pixels never leaves that system, so two runtimes can draw the same scene by different means and nothing crosses.
note: The engine abstracts drawing behind a rendering interface rather than fixing a pipeline, so the pass structure belongs to whichever device is loaded. The earlier statement that the pipeline cannot be inspected no longer holds: the engine, its rendering device and the browser all have public repositories, and the engine's dependency manifest now clones both formerly private libraries from public addresses. The licence picture is uneven and matters to a working group: the engine and the interface SDK are Apache-2.0, the browser's own README calls it proprietary with all rights reserved, and the map library ships no licence file at all.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: A moved scene whose lights are read differently is lit wrong rather than lost.
note: Lighting is now documented in public. Scene-wide ambient and directional light are authored in the manifest's Primary block and are scene properties, not nodes, so a local object cannot alter global illumination; placed point and spot lights are ordinary nodes carrying colour, intensity and cone angles. The composition rule the integration once had to derive from source is now stated: a placed light's intensity is multiplied by the square of its world scale times the scene's flattening scale. There is no indirect light, no shadow model and no probe model anywhere in the format.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: Authored viewpoints are part of a scene, and losing them costs the arrival shot, not the scene.
note: The manifest's Primary block carries one authored camera position and rotation for the default view, and the per-scene flattening also frames the scene for that camera. There is no viewpoint list and no way to move between named viewpoints, and the camera get and set methods reserved in the published interface are marked not implemented, so guest content cannot move the view either.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: If the receiving system cannot rebuild the same tree, parenting and transforms collapse and the asset does not assemble at all.
note: The scene begins at Data.Scene and nests through aChildren arrays; parentage comes from tree position. Each node is a fixed wire record with blocks for head, name, type, owner, resource, transform, orbit, bound and properties. Node handles are per publisher identity rather than scene wide, so the same fabric loaded twice into one container shares one namespace.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: A disagreement about handedness or axis order puts every object in the wrong place or mirrored, which is the classic hand fix.
note: Position, rotation and scale are three, four and three 64-bit floats at fixed offsets in a 528-byte record, and every node composes a full translate-rotate-scale and inherits its parent's, with no class exception. That precision is unusually good. But no handedness and no up axis is declared anywhere in the wire record or the published interface header: the shipped corpus is Z-up purely by convention. The local row records an observed integration failure that no public file states: mounting one of these fabrics into a Y-up host laid the scene on its side with no error, so the integration had to make an up-axis declaration required with no default.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: The file is the boundary: if the second system cannot open it, nothing else on this list matters.
note: The fabric file is the container: a compact JSON Web Signature whose payload holds the serialized manifest under a data claim, with members for container name, declared services and a module list of url and hash pairs, and the scene tree under Data.Scene. The public sample fabric in the engine repository is exactly that, and the browser signs and verifies these files from its own command line.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: A mesh encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a mesh, and the compression choice is where this usually breaks.
note: The format encodes no meshes itself. A node names an external resource by reference and the engine decides what it is by content, parsing a binary or JSON glTF into a render model and treating anything else as an image texture; the tutorial fabrics resolve those references to glTF binary files. Geometry is therefore delegated to a registered format and only the reference is standardised. Two of the vendor's own public notes disagree about what is then drawn: the scene note says the built model is read from the node, while the compositor note says glTF binaries are not parsed there and physical nodes render as boxes for now.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: Layered references are a working convenience, and flattening on export is the fallback that keeps the asset moving.
note: Nested fabrics compose recursively. A node marked as an attachment point starts a fetch of the child fabric, and the parent's scene code parses that child and verifies its signature and chain on its own, so a trusted parent confers nothing on an unverified child. The composition is transclusion, not travel: the child is drawn in the parent's accumulated frame. The local row records an observed property no public file states: cycles and fan-out were proven bounded in this project's working reader.
sources: https://github.com/MetaversalCorp/Sneeze/blob/main/src/context/scene/Scene.md | MSF observed-format note, section 8 (observed bound on cycles and fan-out)

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: A metre read as a centimetre makes the asset useless on arrival, and rescaling by hand is the fix the use case forbids.
note: The wire record declares no units. The engine has since dropped its astronomical-unit path and accumulates all geometry in metres, which removes one trap, but it still gives each scene one flattening factor computed from that scene's own reach, so authored size is not what reaches the screen and a nested child inherits the parent's factor rather than getting its own. The only way to gain precision inside a body is to make that fabric the root. The local row records an observed composition failure that no public file states: a fabric whose native unit was the astronomical unit read as one metre when composed into a one-to-one room, so the integration had to make a units-per-metre value required with no default.
sources: https://github.com/MetaversalCorp/Sneeze/blob/main/src/sneeze/control/Control.md | Open Spatial Lab design note, precision domain (observed composition failure, no public source states it)

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: A signed record of who made an asset lets a receiver trust it; without one the asset still works but nobody can check its history.
note: The signature answers who published these bytes: RS256 over an X.509 chain carried in the JWS header, and the publisher's durable identity is the SHA-256 of the leaf certificate's public key, so it survives certificate renewal. Two cautions, both from the vendor's own public material. The sample fabric shipped in the engine repository is signed by a test certificate authority, not public infrastructure. And the browser does not yet act on the trust it computes: the documentation says the container-open path pins the level instead. The local row records a fact no public file states: a browser-based reader cannot build an X.509 path or read the operating system trust store, so a web reader can only make a labelled claim.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: The portable description of the body is the artefact this use case moves; with no agreement the person arrives as nothing.
note: The fabric describes a place, not a person. The public node classes are root, celestial, terrestrial, physical, panel and light, and there is no skinned mesh, skeleton or appearance description anywhere; the terrestrial property block carries a single avatar flag byte, which is a marker and not a body format. The local row records a fact no public source states: the fabric renderer contract this project built against cannot express a skinned avatar at all, which is why embodiment was kept in a separate lane.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: With no shared wire protocol there is no session to join at all.
note: Fabrics and their assets arrive over ordinary HTTP through the engine's own fetch layer, and the browser can hold a live connection to a map service on a fabric's behalf, so the transport story is no longer only file fetching. Guest content still cannot open a connection of its own: the network fetch method is reserved in the published interface and marked not implemented, the release notes say guest programs run without a network connection, and the intended service-access protocol is described as roadmap. subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: This row is the portal itself, and the travel use case is nothing but the handoff.
note: A portal is a node whose subtype is 255 and whose resource reference is a child fabric URL, and the engine loads the root fabric through the same construct, so root and portal are one type. The engine has no handoff of its own: setting a new address tears down the whole fabric and node tree and rebuilds it, with no camera continuity, no pose transfer and no transition, and the vendor's own note says that doing so while a fabric is still loading is unsafe. The local row records a design decision of this project's integration that no public file states: the two link relations, drawing a child here and travelling to another world, had to be kept deliberately unmerged.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: A roster that does not cross operators means you cannot see who is where, but you can still be there.
note: The fabric is a document. Nothing in the format or the published interface registry describes who else is present, and the vendor's release notes say guest programs run without a network connection in this build.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: A destination name that does not resolve cannot be travelled to, so naming and resolution are the first agreement.
note: A fabric is addressed by an ordinary URL and anyone can host one; the vendor states this plainly in the browser's own release notes. Setting a new address tears the scene down and rebuilds it. The local row records an observed delivery fact no public file states: the shipped artifacts were fetched from a public content network over unauthenticated HTTPS with cross-origin access open.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: Worlds can be reached by a known address, so discovery adds reach rather than making it possible.
note: Discovery is address-based only, and the vendor says so in the browser's own release notes: connecting to what is near you rather than typing an address is on the roadmap, not in the build. The planned service-access layer is likewise described in the documentation as roadmap rather than implemented.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: A shared clock keeps events in order; without one the ordering drifts and coarse clocks still hold the session together.
note: This has changed since the earlier reading and the change is real. The published interface now carries a wall clock and a monotonic clock as first-class subsystems, with a defined base of one sixty-fourth of a second since 1601 in universal time, and a timer service that actually fires: a metronome wakes a timer pool about a thousand times a second and delivers the event back into the guest. What is still absent is the shared part of the capability. Nothing agrees a clock between two publishers or across a network, and the orbit period and origin fields in the wire record still carry no declared unit or zero point, so astronomical time cannot be reproduced from the file alone.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: With no shared base identifier the same person or agent is a stranger in every world they enter.
note: The fabric identifies a publisher, never a person. The engine's own identity object is described by its authors as a temporary local proxy with no network identity and no authentication, used only to scope storage and sandboxes, and personal identity is left to a separate envelope.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: A world that cannot read what an arriving person or agent is allowed to do must either refuse it or trust it blindly.
note: There is no permission grant of any kind in the format or the published interface. The vendor's own documentation separates the two questions plainly, who is this and what may it touch, and then records that the second half is unfinished: the access-control checks exist but the host functions do not yet consistently call them. This is the same hole as the sandbox row seen from the identity side: the manifest can say who signed it and cannot say what the signer is asking for.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: Content pinned to the Earth must land in the same place in the other system, and a pose that cannot be read puts it somewhere else.
note: Positions are Cartesian doubles in the fabric's own frame, with an orbit model for celestial bodies. Nothing expresses a position against the Earth: the public wire record has no geodetic field of any kind, and searching the engine and map libraries for latitude, longitude, a geodetic datum or an earth-centred frame returns nothing. The local row records this project's own unresolved finding on earth-scale coordinate ownership, which no public source states.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: A world that reads controllers differently is harder to use, and pointer and text paths remain.
note: The engine's whole input surface is one viewport structure of mouse deltas, a scroll value, two mouse buttons and eight key flags, and it belongs to the application rather than to content. Nothing reaches guest content: the published interface registry has no input, event, pointer, pick or navigate subsystem, and the one viewport subsystem it does reserve is camera get and set, marked not implemented. The vendor's release notes say headset and hand tracking are not ready in this build. Any interactive spatial standard that assumes content can be picked will not compose with this.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: The language a world writes its rules in is its own business and never has to cross.
note: World rules are WebAssembly modules listed in the manifest and optionally hash-pinned. The published interface header is now the normative contract: the guest provides Init, Open, Close and Shutdown plus Alloc, Free and Notify, and every guest-to-host request crosses one import called Call, carrying a packet whose subsystem and method are numbers. The vendor's stated reason is that a module compiled once keeps loading as the engine grows, because a new method is a new number rather than a new symbol.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: The use case says the asset must behave, so a door that will not open in the second system is the failure this row names.
note: There is no declarative interactivity that travels with a fabric. The one seam worth naming is now weaker than the earlier reading recorded: the 528-byte node record still reserves a 64-bit event field in its head, the node decoder still defines a constant for the matching Event key, and no code path in the engine reads or writes that field. Nodes whose resource reference begins with an action scheme are treated as invisible helpers and the only thing the compositor does with them is decline to draw them.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: A host can sandbox guest content on its own; agreement only makes the limits predictable for the guest.
note: Real isolation exists and is documented: each module instance gets its own linear memory, and console, storage and network handles are scoped to the publisher's identity so one source cannot read another's cached files, stored documents or log stream. What is missing is the permission half. There is no grant, scope or capability of any kind in the interface registry, and the vendor's own documentation says the access-control checks are defined but the host functions do not yet consistently call them. The ownership functions are present in the engine source and no caller anywhere in the tree calls them. A signature says who wrote the code and has never said what the code may do.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: Without agreed limits, guest content and agents are throttled or refused unpredictably.
note: No fuel, no memory cap and no storage quota are applied to guest content. The evidence is the vendor's own: the documentation lists resource limits as planned and states that fuel and memory limits are proven but not yet applied per source, and the only place fuel metering appears in the engine tree is a test.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: What survives a restart is mostly the host's business; it crosses the boundary only when a visitor's changes must last.
note: Guest content gets four storage scopes in the published interface: permanent and temporary, each in an organisation and a container variant. Isolation is cryptographic rather than by name, because the organisation tier is keyed by the publisher's certificate fingerprint, which is the hash of the signing public key. It is correct incidentally rather than normatively, there is no quota, and nothing in the format says what a world must persist.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: Naming content by hash makes an item the same item everywhere; without it copies drift while still loading.
note: Modules may be pinned by an exact SHA-256 in the manifest, in the subresource-integrity spelling, and the fetch layer refuses a body whose digest does not match. The hole is structural and is provable from the public source: the manifest reader takes the hash only if the key is present, the verifier returns success when the hash string is empty, and public sample fabrics in both the engine repository and the tutorial documentation ship modules with no hash at all. A validly signed manifest may therefore cover the manifest but not the module bytes.

subject: RP1 Spatial Fabric
interop_reason: A runnable experience moves between hosts far less often than an asset does, and repackaging is the fallback.
note: One signed file carries the manifest, the module list with hashes, the declared services and the scene, so a fabric is a complete runnable package behind one URL. The media type is unsettled and unregistered: the browser's own source matches the label application/jose+msf, and the official registry lists application/jose and application/jose+json from RFC 7515 but nothing for a spatial fabric. The local row records this project's own label, which no public source states.

note: The pinned compute module dispatches SPIR-V kernels through Vox with registered CPU fallbacks; unrestricted guest access is not claimed.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: How a system turns geometry into pixels never leaves that system, so two runtimes can draw the same scene by different means and nothing crosses.
note: It streams from a host engine rather than specifying one: the protocol is an application-layer network protocol and names no rasterizer. It does constrain what a renderer must accept, since materials, textures, meshes and text canvases all have wire formats, but the pipeline itself is the implementation's business.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Labels, signs and name tags lose their font and layout when the two systems disagree, so the text degrades while the rest of the asset is fine.
note: Text in three dimensions has two payload types of its own, a font atlas holding glyph-position metadata keyed by point size and a text canvas holding the renderable contents, so legible text is a protocol concern rather than an application one.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: If the receiving system cannot rebuild the same tree, parenting and transforms collapse and the asset does not assemble at all.
note: A node is an object positioned in three dimensions that may have child nodes forming a hierarchy, delivered as its own payload type with a fixed-size header, an optional component record, an explicit remove-nodes payload and a resource lifecycle. Nodes are also how per-client state enters the scene: one node is named as a client's origin, the frame its tracking is measured from.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A disagreement about handedness or axis order puts every object in the wrong place or mirrored, which is the classic hand fix.
note: Handedness and vertical axis are negotiated rather than assumed. The client declares its native axes in the handshake, the server publishes the axes its scene is authored in, and every server-to-client packet carrying geometry is already converted into the client's standard. The standard is a one-byte value with four complete named combinations and discriminator bits so that no two are the same byte, and a server must support at least the engineering and OpenGL styles. Assets fetched over HTTP are the exception: they are served as authored and the pointer chunk declares which frame they are in, so the client converts. Transforms are local to the parent, and a root node is expressed directly in the server's global space.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: The file is the boundary: if the second system cannot open it, nothing else on this list matters.
note: The protocol states outright that Teleport has no file format, and that the Teleport network is part of the Internet but not part of the Web. A node here is a changing object inside a live stream with no URL, not addressable from outside the session, where a world-addressing API means a fetchable, editable record by the same name. Anyone building a bridge between the two meets this on the first day. One qualification since 2026-06-16: most geometry now arrives as a mesh pointer, a URL the client fetches and decodes by file extension, so ordinary asset files do cross the boundary even though the scene itself has no document form.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A mesh encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a mesh, and the compression choice is where this usually breaks.
note: Meshes are a first-class payload type on the geometry channel, with a pointer form for fetching one over HTTP and reusing an already-delivered resource. One constraint a working group should note: only Draco compression is emitted, and uncompressed meshes are not supported on the wire.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Device-specific texture compression is the common failure: the model arrives untextured and someone must re-export it.
note: Textures are their own payload type with a pointer form for reuse, and large ones are normally promoted to the pointer form and fetched over HTTP rather than sent inline.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Carrying materials without loss is what "renders in another system" means, and only two subjects reach this row natively today.
note: A material payload carries a metallic-roughness description with a list of extension records, and textures it names travel as their own chunks, so a material does cross between implementations. What does not work is the per-object variation: the MaterialInstance payload type exists in the enumeration but is reserved, is not emitted, and has an unspecified body that receivers must skip. An earlier claim in this row that a shared definition and its per-object variations travel independently was wrong and is withdrawn.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A clip that cannot be read leaves the object still, and an avatar that cannot move is not an avatar.
note: Animation is a payload type on the geometry channel, carrying per-bone keyframe tracks, and clips are more usually delivered out of band as files through an animation pointer.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: The bone hierarchy is what makes a body move correctly elsewhere; without an agreed one, motion has nothing to bind to.
note: A skeleton payload is the ordered list of bone-node identifiers making up a skeletal hierarchy, and the bones themselves are ordinary scene nodes. A mesh names the skeleton it is skinned to and maps its own bones onto it, with an explicit marker for an unmapped bone. It is the only subject in this group that carries a rig at all.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A metre read as a centimetre makes the asset useless on arrival, and rescaling by hand is the fix the use case forbids.
note: The protocol declares the unit outright: linear units are metres. That single sentence is the thing every other subject in this group is missing, and it sits in the same conventions chapter as the axis negotiation, so scale and orientation are settled together before any geometry moves.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: The portable description of the body is the artefact this use case moves; with no agreement the person arrives as nothing.
note: Avatars are negotiated rather than defined, and the negotiation has grown teeth since 2026-06-16. The server advertises a policy; the reference structure for that policy now carries first-class limits for accepted formats, file size, triangle count, height and width in metres, texture count and total texture pixels, a named skeleton, and a list of allowed licence tags. The client offers a URL with a declared format and byte count, and the server accepts or refuses and says whether delivery is by relay or by import. A relayed URL must end in a recognised extension because clients pick a decoder by extension; the extensions named are glTF binary, VRM and glTF. The avatar file's own contents remain out of scope.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Without a way to bind an avatar to a verifiable identity, the person who arrives cannot be shown to be the person who left.
note: This is the row that changed most since 2026-06-16, and it is the single most consequential change in the subject. An avatar offer may now name a signed Universal Manifest instead of a bare asset address, and the server reads the asset address out of the verified manifest. The reference server ships the resolver, verifies Signature Profile A (Ed25519 over RFC 8785 canonical JSON with the signature member removed), gates every facet by the subject's own consent records with default-deny, caches on the manifest's own expiry rather than the HTTP response, and returns a structured receipt to the client saying what it did with the document. Two limits are stated by the implementers themselves and both matter: only trust tier zero, signature-only, is actually verified, and verification deliberately does not check that the manifest's subject is the client presenting it, so a verified manifest is authentic but not proof of the bearer's right to it. The older empty proof registry is still there in the signalling document, and mid-session revocation remains real.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Positioned sounds are authored into a scene, and losing them leaves a silent room.
note: Positioning a sound is now a single rule and it is a good one: the outbound track's session-description identifier is set to the decimal uid of the node that emits the sound, and that is the only binding between the audio transport and the scene. Identifier zero, or one naming a node the client cannot place, plays without position, so an announcer or a music bed needs no node. Because that identifier cannot change for the life of a media line, the binding is stable for the whole session. The earlier claim in this row, that an audio source mapping command binds streams to places, is withdrawn: that command is now reserved and servers must not send it.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: How direction is turned into sound at the ears is the receiving system's method, like a rendering method.
note: The protocol says where a sound is and refuses to say how it should reach the ears. A track bound to a placed node is spatialised by the client at that node's world transform, and the layering is explicit: the server decides whether a listener receives a track, the client decides how loud. Gain and rolloff are client or application defaults and are deliberately not carried on the wire, so two conformant clients in the same room may attenuate the same voice differently. There is no head-related transfer function, no ambisonic model, no room acoustics and no occlusion.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A visitor can be given audio by other means, so disagreement costs quality and scale.
note: Audio has a full chapter: Opus with named defaults for payload type, sample rate, channels, frame duration, forward error correction and discontinuous transmission, a selective forwarding topology, a seventeen-byte configuration block inside the setup command, a per-listener cap with five named selection policies, and a lifecycle. Codec, sample rate and channel count cannot be changed mid-session.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A visitor who cannot be heard is diminished but still present, and text remains a fallback.
note: Live voice between participants is carried by the same audio chapter. In a room session the server is a selective forwarding unit: each microphone arrives on one inbound track and a chosen subset is forwarded to every other listener as separate outbound tracks, with loopback suppression required and hysteresis recommended before a speaker is dropped from a listener's set.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A client or agent that cannot read the destination's state stream arrives blind, which ends both use cases on the spot.
note: State moves as command packets from server to client and message packets from client to server, over a setup command, a handshake and then updates. Ordering tools are per message and work identically on both reliable transports: an acknowledgement identifier that increases monotonically per session, and a separately acknowledged confirmation number on node state.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Disagreement about who owns an arriving object shows up as rubber-banding and contested edits rather than as a failed arrival.
note: The server owns the ground truth of the simulation. It may grant a client control of particular nodes, for example the client's own head and hands, but it stays the final arbiter, and it also decides what the client's control inputs mean.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Without agreement the destination sends everything or too little, which costs scale.
note: Interest management is the design centre: worlds are never downloaded whole, the server tells each client which nodes and resources to track, and two clients on one server may hold entirely different sets.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: With no shared wire protocol there is no session to join at all.
note: Three layers in parallel: a WebSocket for signalling, WebRTC by default for real-time streams with optional legacy SRT and EFP, and HTTP or HTTPS for static assets. Reliable payloads must work over either the WebSocket or the WebRTC reliable channel and receivers must accept both for the whole session. One caution for an implementer: the normative channel table says five SCTP data channels and three other places in the same documentation set say six, so the count is not settled in the text; channels are matched by label, and five labels are defined.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Live audio and video degrade or drop out while the visit continues.
note: Video and audio ride WebRTC media tracks. Audio is Opus with the payload type, sample rate, channel count, frame duration, forward error correction and discontinuous transmission all published in a seventeen-byte block inside the setup command, and both sides must advertise and honour those values in the session description. Video has its own chapters for frame structure, metadata and recovery.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Joining a running world, authentication included, is the door: no agreement, no entry.
note: A full connection state machine with four named phases, reconnection, timeouts and an enumerated state list. The client repeats a connect message until it gets a response carrying a client and server identifier as unsigned 64-bit numbers; a matching server identifier lets cached resource and node identifiers persist across a reconnect, though the client may not assume it. Authentication of the asset service is still deliberately outside the protocol: the HTTP service is shared by every connected client with no per-client authentication. Since 2026-06-16 the reference implementations have added a session-level identity handshake on the signalling channel, which the protocol document does not yet describe; see identity.root.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: This row is the portal itself, and the travel use case is nothing but the handoff.
note: There is no crossing between servers and no arrival with state intact. A search of the whole published documentation for the portaling standard, its standards body, the word portal and any form of interoperate returns nothing, and the chapter list confirms no such chapter exists. Whether an inter-world destination address could legitimately be a teleport URL is an open composition question that nobody owns; that framing is the project's own reading and has no public source.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A roster that does not cross operators means you cannot see who is where, but you can still be there.
note: Presence is inferred from the scene, not announced. Another client arrives as an ordinary node on the geometry channel, and a voice arrives as an audio track whose session-description identifier is the decimal uid of the node that emits it. The protocol states outright that no signalling message tells a client anything about another client's avatar, and that client identifiers are never exposed to other clients. Two earlier claims in this row have been retracted: the peer message form and the audio participant state change command are both withdrawn upstream, and the command identifiers for AudioSourceMapping and AudioParticipantStateChange are now reserved with servers forbidden to send them.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A destination name that does not resolve cannot be travelled to, so naming and resolution are the first agreement.
note: A client is launched with a teleport URL and the path inside it identifies the requested session on the server; the WebSocket is opened at that host, port and path, and the path may be empty. That is a launch address, not a naming or resolution system, and the port is by convention rather than assignment.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Worlds can be reached by a known address, so discovery adds reach rather than making it possible.
note: Discovery is a named phase of the session state machine and its content is that there is none: the client locates a server by some out-of-band mechanism, a typed URL, a name lookup or browser navigation, and resolves it to a WebSocket address. Nothing in the protocol finds a server for you, and the port is by convention.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A shared clock keeps events in order; without one the ordering drifts and coarse clocks still hold the session together.
note: Time is in microseconds. The setup command carries the session start as a server wall-clock value in Unix time and every other time on the wire is an offset from it, with a ping and pong pair for latency. The limit is stated plainly: the client's own session-relative timestamps are monotonic within one session and are not comparable across clients or to any wall clock, so this is a session clock rather than a shared ordering guarantee between participants.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: With no shared base identifier the same person or agent is a stranger in every world they enter.
note: The published protocol document and the reference implementations no longer agree, and an implementer should know which one they are building against. The signalling chapter still says the identity member is an opaque string supplied for application-level authentication that may be empty. Both reference servers now treat that bare string as a legacy shape and accept an object with a provider, an issuer, a subject and a display name, sorted into three trust levels: anonymous, asserted, and verified. Asserted gets its own keyspace precisely because anyone can claim anyone's subject; verified keys derive only from the token's own claims and never from anything the client typed. Two new signalling message types, identity-challenge and identity-response, carry the freshness proof. None of this is in the protocol document.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Claims about age, membership or ownership are worthless if the receiving world cannot read them.
note: This row was scored none and that is no longer true. The reference server now has a credential verification registry keyed by credential type, with a named list of the schemes a server might accept: an OpenID Connect identity token, a plain OAuth2 access token, a W3C verifiable credential or decentralized identifier proof, and a SAML assertion. One of the four is implemented; the rest are left to host applications. The implemented one is careful: the identity token is bound to a long-lived client key by putting the key's thumbprint in the token's nonce, and a live challenge-response proves the presenter holds that key, so a token captured by one server cannot be replayed at another. TeleportXR still defines no credential format of its own. An earlier claim in this row, that the words consent, trust, permission, provenance, encryption and credential were all absent from the project, no longer holds and is withdrawn.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A credential nobody can ask for or present is not a credential, and one subject reaches this row natively today.
note: There is now a real request-and-present exchange, for one purpose. The server states a policy, the client presents a signed manifest address, the server verifies and answers with an accept or refuse plus a structured receipt naming every facet it read, skipped or refused. That is a credential presentation protocol in all but name. Two things keep it short of the capability: it is scoped to the avatar asset class, and the chapter that specifies it, avatar_manifest, is referenced by the chapter list, by the signalling chapter and by the C++ headers, but the file does not exist in the public repository.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A world that cannot read what an arriving person or agent is allowed to do must either refuse it or trust it blindly.
note: Permission is read, not defined. Where a deployment turns on the manifest option, the server evaluates the subject's own consent records before it uses any part of the document, and the rule is default-deny: a facet with no consent entry naming it is recorded as consent-missing and its data must not be processed. The exception is deliberate and stated: an unstated reference is permitted for the avatar pointer itself, because consent in that model is defined over facets and demanding one per pointer would reject every manifest in circulation. This is an optional profile carried in the avatar policy, not part of the base protocol, so it is scored via-extension.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Content pinned to the Earth must land in the same place in the other system, and a pose that cannot be read puts it somewhere else.
note: Nothing places a session or a node against the Earth. Positions are simulation-local and server-owned, and no chapter in the published documentation mentions a geographic pose, a coordinate reference system, latitude or an Earth model. The only frame the protocol negotiates is the client's axis convention.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A world that reads controllers differently is harder to use, and pointer and text paths remain.
note: Input is negotiated rather than fixed. The server declares the inputs it expects as a list of identifier, type and path, where the path is a regular expression matched against the client's own control paths, and the client decides which physical control satisfies each one. A new declaration replaces the previous set wholesale and invalidates every earlier identifier.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A world that cannot ask what the arriving device can do will guess, and guessing wrong costs quality rather than entry.
note: Two mechanisms exist and one of them is empty. The server does tell the client which control inputs it expects, and the client declares its axes standard in the handshake, so the parts that matter for drawing and for input do flow. But the general capability bag on the connect message has no defined keys at all: it is an extension point with a rule that unknown keys must be ignored, and the conventions chapter says plainly that there is no formal capability negotiation beyond the rendering features flag and the session-description exchange. This row was previously scored native; that overstated it.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: The language a world writes its rules in is its own business and never has to cross.
note: Guest code has no place in this model. The application lives on the server and the client is a view into it; nothing in the documentation names a scripting language, a sandbox or a resource budget for guest content.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: An agent with no agreed way to perceive and act in a world it did not come from cannot join it at all.
note: There is no agent inside the world, but since 2026-06-16 there is a documented way for one to drive a client from outside. A headless client runs as a daemon and a line-oriented control protocol on a loopback socket lets a terminal, a script, a continuous-integration job or a language-model agent issue one command and read one response. It is explicitly not the streaming protocol and it has no authentication, on the stated ground that anything able to open a loopback socket already has the user's shell. Nothing in the world protocol distinguishes a person from a program.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: What survives a restart is mostly the host's business; it crosses the boundary only when a visitor's changes must last.
note: Deliberately excluded. How the server stores its data is stated as entirely implementation-dependent, and there is no world file to survive a restart. What does survive is client-side: the reference client keeps a warm geometry cache keyed by session identifier, and a reconnect to the same server session may keep cached resource and node identifiers.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: The use case names inventory, and items that cannot be read at the destination do not travel with the person.
note: Nothing carries items today, but the shape of an answer is now published and marked as not yet real. A chapter added since 2026-06-16 sketches three classes of portable asset: the avatar, an object borne into the world, and an object held in an inventory and not currently in the scene. The chapter opens by saying it is a design sketch and that only the avatar case is specified and implemented. Two rules in it are worth a working group's attention even in sketch form: a proof must bind the holder to the specific assets it covers, and coverage must be enumerated inside the signed payload rather than taken from the client's routing hint.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Naming content by hash makes an item the same item everywhere; without it copies drift while still loading.
note: Content hashing is used at two named points and is not a general scheme. An avatar offer and a peer relay carry a content hash beside the URL so a peer can check it fetched the file the owner meant. Separately the client's asset cache is keyed by URL, and the specification places the obligation on the server: publish each immutable asset at a unique, stable URL. That is addressing by location with a contract, not addressing by hash.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Assets reach clients over ordinary web delivery, so agreement here buys scale and cost rather than possibility.
note: Assets come over ordinary HTTP but the protocol explicitly pushes the usual web delivery machinery outside itself: resource expiry, entity tag handling, range requests and authentication are all stated as not part of the protocol, and the service is shared by every client. That collides with a world-addressing standard in the same stack whose asset pillar is built out of exactly those things, entity tags, conditional requests and per-request authorisation. Two specifications a client would have to satisfy at once take opposite positions on whether HTTP caching semantics are in scope.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A reader that cannot tell which version it holds, or what to do with the parts it does not know, breaks on the first update, which is the "no hand fixes" test again.
note: A versioning section in the conventions chapter, a protocol version carried in the connect message, still 0.9, and a forward-compatibility rule that unknown capability keys and unrecognised members must be ignored. The hard edge is stated too: the payload-type and codec enumerations are part of the wire format, so adding a value is a breaking change that must bump the protocol version, and endpoints that disagree on the version should drop the connection rather than negotiate. Do not confuse this with the client release numbers: the repository has published tagged client releases from v2.0 to v2.8 since 2026-08-02 while the protocol version stayed at 0.9.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Every other must row is a claim until a shared test says it holds, which is exactly what the meeting asked for.
note: Normative keywords are used throughout, which gives it a conformance vocabulary that the world-addressing standard in the same stack does not have, and reference implementations exist for client and server in two languages. There is still no conformance suite and no independent evaluation, and the project labels its own work pre-alpha. Two changes since 2026-06-16 pull in opposite directions. The good one: the canonicalisation code is now held to a shared cross-language vector set, so a document signed by the Node server must verify on the C++ one, which is the first real interoperability test in this subject. The bad one: the chapter list names a chapter, avatar_manifest, that does not exist in the repository, and two other files cross-reference it, so the specification for the identity mechanism described above is not published.

subject: TeleportXR
capability: World generation from a prompt or an image
interop_reason: A generated place that arrives only as frames to watch still reaches the viewer, but as a recording rather than a world the receiver can open and use.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and making a whole three-dimensional place from a description or a picture is not an act it performs or specifies.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A world continued by a model still reaches a viewer, but only as what the model chooses to show, so the receiver cannot keep it or run it again.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and it never continues a world under a viewer's actions from a learned model; there is no such model here.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: How a system turns photographs into a model is its own method, and what leaves is an ordinary asset the container and geometry rows already carry.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and turning a set of ordinary photographs into a textured three-dimensional model is not among its jobs.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so this row is what geometry encoding is for a mesh: splat content in a named format the receiving tool cannot read does not arrive at all, and re-exporting it is the hand fix the use case forbids.
note: The protocol states outright that it has no file format, so there is nothing for a named splat interchange format to be. Geometry crosses as protocol chunks, and the only compression named for them is Draco.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Without an agreed order for what arrives first, a large capture still loads, it just makes the viewer wait for the whole of it.
note: This subject streams a scene by need, which is close enough to the row to be worth stating clearly, and it streams an authored, server-held simulation rather than a capture: meshes arrive as compressed geometry chunks on a channel, keyed to what the client can see. There is no captured scene, no detail ladder over one and no region ordering for one.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a volumetric clip is an asset like any other: without the calibration and mask metadata a second implementation needs, what arrives is not the recording and no one can make it one by hand.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and it carries no captured, time-varying three-dimensional scene as media, and no camera calibration or mask metadata for one.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a point cloud encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a point cloud, exactly as an undecodable mesh is not a mesh, and that capture shows nothing.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and it defines no encoding or compression for a set of points with attributes.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so views that arrive without their intrinsics and extrinsics cannot be reprojected: the capture lands as loose pictures rather than as the place it recorded.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and it carries no set of calibrated camera views with per-pixel depth, and no intrinsics or extrinsics to reproject them.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Making an image from a viewpoint no camera occupied is a method inside one system, and what crosses to a second system is the picture it produced.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and it produces no image from a viewing position that no capture camera occupied.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a moving capture handed over as unrelated frames is not the capture: the receiver has to guess the rate and the ordering the sender already knew, and guessing is the hand fix the use case forbids.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and it carries no captured scene that changes over time, and states no rate at which one should be played back.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Whether a captured scene answers the light around it is work the receiving system does, and the asset arrives either way.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and it holds no captured scene that could be made to answer the light of the place it lands in.

subject: TeleportXR
capability: Editing a capture after the fact
interop_reason: Editing a capture happens in the tool that holds it, and what leaves is the edited asset, which the format rows already carry.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and there is no capture here to crop, delete from or recolour, and no export for such an edit to survive.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Describing a change to a world you already made is one service's own interface, and the world that results still leaves by the ordinary export rows.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and there is no generated world here to change by describing the change or pointing at a region.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A generator that cannot read the specification another tool wrote still produces a world, it just will not be the world that was asked for.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and nothing here accepts a specification of a world that should be made.

subject: TeleportXR
capability: Deriving conventional assets from a generated scene
interop_reason: Derived meshes and panoramas are how a generated world reaches a conventional engine at all, and each route loses something the receiver has to be told about.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and it derives no collision mesh, drawing mesh, panorama or video from a splat or radiance-field world.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Actions that arrive without their embodiment, frame and units cannot be replayed elsewhere, so an agent acts only in the system it was written for.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and it carries no agent's actions in or out as time-sampled data with an embodiment, a frame and units.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A panorama whose projection is not stated is still an image, but the receiver has to guess before it can use it as a backdrop or as a light.
note: TeleportXR is a session protocol in which a server holds the truth and each client is sent only the slice of state it needs now, and it carries no full 360-degree view of a place as an image with its projection stated.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A reconstruction that cannot leave the device that made it keeps the room private to one session, so anything placed against it has to be fitted again elsewhere.
note: The protocol names augmented and mixed reality among its targets, yet everything flows one way: the server holds the ground truth and sends nodes, meshes and materials down to the client. There is no message in which a client reports the shape of the room it is standing in, so a reconstruction made on the device has nowhere to go.

subject: TeleportXR
capability: Semantic labelling of the real world
interop_reason: Labels each vendor names differently still serve one application, but a second one cannot act on floor or sky without being rewritten for that vendor.
note: The client-to-server channel is a dynamic input model of buttons, axes and poses the server asks for. No label for a real surface is among the things a client may report, and the server has no way to ask for one.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Depth reported in units the receiver does not share puts real surfaces at the wrong distance, so content is placed badly rather than not at all.
note: Depth in this protocol runs the wrong way: the video stream's alpha channel carries the depth of the scene the server rendered, as a cubemap for reprojection on the client. Nothing carries the depth of the real room from the client to the server.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Whether real surfaces hide virtual content is drawn on the device that sees them, and none of that decision crosses to a second system.
note: With no real-world depth or geometry crossing the connection, the protocol says nothing about hiding streamed content behind real surfaces, even though it claims mixed reality as a target.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: How much of the real room a runtime lets through is its own presentation, and an arriving asset cannot tell the difference.
note: The server renders and streams a cubemap to the client, with the scene's depth packed into the alpha channel so the client can reproject it. Depth in alpha is what a compositor would need to blend with a camera view, and the protocol never takes that step: there is no blend mode, no passthrough layer and no way for the server to say how much of the room should show.

subject: TeleportXR
capability: Face and body tracking as input
interop_reason: A face and body stream in a shape the receiver does not read leaves the avatar still rather than absent, and its privacy terms have to be agreed with it.
note: Input travels the other way as named control paths matched against the client's own controls, which is a controller and hand model. There is no face or body stream in the input protocol and no privacy terms for one.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A place that arrives without its walkable surface and arrival points still loads, but whoever opens it has to work out where a body may stand and where a portal lands.
note: The client receives a rendered stream and a geometry payload for what it draws locally. Where a body may stand is decided on the server, inside whichever engine is running the world, and never crosses the protocol.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A published unit of logic whose name resolves to something else elsewhere still runs, but nobody can be sure which code they called.
note: Logic stays on the server; the client is given geometry and video. Nothing is published as a unit of logic under a name that another author would depend on.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A receiving world that cannot tell what review arriving content has already had still shows it, and has to repeat the whole review itself.
note: A remote rendering protocol carries frames between one server and one client it has already connected to. There is no publishing path to an audience in which a review could stand.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Two maps of one place with no published transform between them put the same content in two positions, so a person arrives beside where they meant to be.
note: The protocol has no geographic frame and no map of a real place.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A service that never declares where it applies still answers, so a client has to call it and find out instead of testing whether it is relevant.
note: A server is found by an out-of-band address, not by the region it covers, and it declares no area of application.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A receiver must distinguish required additions from optional ones or it cannot safely interpret an arriving asset or exchange.
note: The draft signaling protocol declares a capabilities object and requires unknown keys and unrecognized content members to be ignored; feature keys are not yet assigned.

subject: TeleportXR
capability: Domain metadata carried with an asset
interop_reason: An asset can load without shared descriptive properties, but receivers lose the classifications and facts that drive its use.
note: Teleport's node payload declares typed descriptive name, stationary state, holder client ID and streaming-priority fields alongside the scene-node record, with wire types and meanings for the receiver.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: A scene or visit can continue when interface layouts differ, but carried controls and information may become hard to use.
note: Teleport's TextCanvas/FontAtlas protocol carries text, point size, line height, glyph placement and advance in local canvas units, attached to a transformed scene node. These define the presented 2D text region.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: An asset with external resources cannot load intact if the receiver cannot resolve its resource references in the intended context.
note: TexturePointer and MeshPointer resolve resource payloads through HTTP(S) URLs; MaterialPointer remains reserved.

subject: TeleportXR
capability: Pose series and live pose streams
interop_reason: Systems exchanging moving subjects must agree on the time and frame of each pose or the subject's movement cannot be reconstructed correctly.
note: The draft client-to-server protocol sends timestamped ControllerPoses with head and controller position/orientation data; this is protocol coverage, not a live runtime test.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Without agreed links and transform meaning, receivers cannot reconstruct the same related frames for transferred content or participants.
note: The draft node payload exchanges local transforms with parent identifiers so receivers reconstruct the linked hierarchy in the negotiated axes.

subject: TeleportXR
capability: Frame pacing and predicted display time
interop_reason: Disagreement between an arriving application and the device runtime about display timing degrades the view through stale poses or poor frame pacing.
note: Server render timestamps and camera transforms are associated with video frames for reprojection. They are not a predicted headset display-time contract.

subject: TeleportXR
interop_reason: Without shared sensed-data disclosure terms, content, avatars, travellers and agents can still operate but may expose more data than intended.
note: Teleport gates client-to-server microphone capture with SetupCommand.audio_input_enabled and limits voice distribution per listener. These are explicit sensed-data disclosure controls.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: How a system turns geometry into pixels never leaves that system, so two runtimes can draw the same scene by different means and nothing crosses.
note: Web of Worlds describes how a world is addressed and what it reports about itself. It draws nothing and names no renderer; the one field about rendering technology records which engine the world was built with, as free text.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Authored viewpoints are part of a scene, and losing them costs the arrival shot, not the scene.
note: A View resource exists with its own path and a geoPose, and a URL fragment can preview a named aspect, so viewpoints are addressable. Nothing describes projection, field of view, near and far planes, or how a viewer moves between views.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: If the receiving system cannot rebuild the same tree, parenting and transforms collapse and the asset does not assemble at all.
note: The graph is described twice and the two descriptions disagree. Node.children is an array of embedded Node objects, so a subtree is carried inline, while Node.parent is a bare integer, so the same relationship is also expressible by reference; neither is required, no precedence is stated, and nothing says what a server should do when both are present. The project's own integration served a flat identifier-reference node instead, and before that divergence was declared a write with embedded children was answered 200 OK with its whole subtree silently deleted. That last observation is the project's own and has no public source.
sources: https://github.com/WebOfWorlds/WoWAPI/blob/main/specification/OpenSpatialWorld/API.yaml | OSL to Web of Worlds contract, divergence D7

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A disagreement about handedness or axis order puts every object in the wrong place or mirrored, which is the classic hand fix.
note: Node.localTransform is an array of number with no declared length and no declared major order, and no world declares an up axis or a handedness anywhere. When a real Z-up fabric was mounted into this Y-up graph the scene silently lay on its side, so the project's integration added a required up-axis field with no default and refuses the node when it is missing; that repair is local and has no public source.
sources: https://github.com/WebOfWorlds/WoWAPI/blob/main/specification/OpenSpatialWorld/API.yaml | OSL to Web of Worlds contract, divergence D7

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: The file is the boundary: if the second system cannot open it, nothing else on this list matters.
note: The asset API standardises content negotiation over twenty-one registered model media types, including glTF, USD, X3D, COLLADA, OBJ, STL and STEP, but defines no container of its own and has no type for a signed or executable spatial document. Node.spatialAssetURI is a bare string with no format, no media type and no prose, so any URL is legal and nothing says what it resolves to.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Layered references are a working convenience, and flattening on export is the fallback that keeps the asset moving.
note: A Spatial descriptor names a root node and the node tree nests, but the recursion is over nodes inside one world and never over worlds: there is no sub-world, no cross-world reference and no override or layering vocabulary anywhere in the three files.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A metre read as a centimetre makes the asset useless on arrival, and rescaling by hand is the fix the use case forbids.
note: No world declares units, scale or extent. The World schema carries a label, an age restriction, a licence, a cost, a version and a duration and nothing dimensional, so metre scale is an assumption that is never stated and a renderer has nothing to compute a bound from. Composing an astronomical-unit fabric into a one-to-one metre world therefore read one astronomical unit as one metre; that repair, a required units-per-metre field with no default, is the project's own and has no public source.
