subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: An item that arrives with no readable terms cannot be lawfully worn, shown or sold, so the move fails at the rights boundary even when every byte arrives.
note: A world carries content.license, content.cost and content.age_restriction, all untyped strings or numbers with no vocabulary, and the asset resource repeats the same three fields. There is no licence identifier scheme and nothing a recipient can act on mechanically.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A signed record of who made an asset lets a receiver trust it; without one the asset still works but nobody can check its history.
note: The graph is live unsigned JSON. There is no signature, integrity or provenance vocabulary in any of the three files; the only integrity-adjacent header is an entity tag, described as revision control for caching. This is exactly where the RP1 fabric met it cleanly in the project's integration: the fabric arrives already signed and hash-pinned, so the address rides in the Web of Worlds field while the trust claim rides entirely in the fabric.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: The portable description of the body is the artefact this use case moves; with no agreement the person arrives as nothing.
note: A user carries an avatar address and the user manifest repeats it, but nothing says what format it points at, how it is rigged, or what scale it is in. The address is the whole of the avatar model.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Mass and velocity carried across make a moved object behave nearly the same; their absence changes the behaviour without stopping it.
note: No simulation model of any kind. The single related field is a free string named gravity inside the world's presence object.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: How direction is turned into sound at the ears is the receiving system's method, like a rendering method.
note: Sound is not mentioned anywhere in the three files. The World schema's nearest neighbours are avatar, navigation and gravity, all free strings.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A client or agent that cannot read the destination's state stream arrives blind, which ends both use cases on the spot.
note: Nothing in the three specification files says which state is shared, how often, or in what form. The reference implementation's WebSocket event stream is a convention that implementation invented; it is not in the OpenAPI contract and no message shape for it is published.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: With no shared wire protocol there is no session to join at all.
note: HTTP 1.1 carries the whole contract and is cited by reference. Nothing in the specification carries live session traffic. The reference implementation adds a WebSocket events route at /events, which is real and public but sits outside the machine-readable contract, so its messages bypass the validator.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Joining a running world, authentication included, is the door: no agreement, no entry.
note: Joining is specified as visiting the URL, with fragments distinguishing join, follow and preview; the user manifest API uses a HEAD request to authorise a resource and returns 403 or 404. There is no authentication scheme, no session token and no session lifecycle. The asset README names end-to-end authorisation and modern single sign-on as a requirement, but no machine-readable file defines one.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: This row is the portal itself, and the travel use case is nothing but the handoff.
note: Portals exist as addressable resources and the join fragment defines arrival as a new or existing user, but the canonical Portal carries only an identifier and a geoPose, so it cannot say where it leads; there is no crossing protocol and no state transfer. This is the exact complement of the OMA3 portaling specification, which specifies the crossing and has no object to hang it on. The proposal to type the missing destination as a portaling URI is the project's own and has no public source.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A roster that does not cross operators means you cannot see who is where, but you can still be there.
note: A world reports active and total user counts, view counts and portal counts, and a user resource carries a pose, so a crude roster can be derived. There is no cross-operator presence and no join or leave event in the contract. Note a naming trap: the field actually called presence is not about who is present at all, it holds three free strings for avatar, navigation and gravity.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A destination name that does not resolve cannot be travelled to, so naming and resolution are the first agreement.
note: The core of the subject: a world is a URL, joined, followed and previewed by URL fragment, and its parts hang off that same URL as URL/wow/world and URL/wow/user/4182. The whitepaper states the idea directly and the world README turns it into the five core requirements.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Worlds can be reached by a known address, so discovery adds reach rather than making it possible.
note: There is no registry, no index and no way to find a world you do not already have the URL for. The complete path list of the world API is a web app at the root, one world resource, one user, one view, one portal and the spatial graph; none of them lists or searches anything.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: With no shared base identifier the same person or agent is a stranger in every world they enter.
note: A user is an integer in a path with no issuer and no namespace, so two worlds cannot mean the same person. The whitepaper and the Forum's own announcement both name decentralized identifiers as the foundation of the portable identity layer, but no decentralized identifier appears anywhere in the machine-readable text.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Claims about age, membership or ownership are worthless if the receiving world cannot read them.
note: The user manifest carries a name, an age and an avatar address and nothing else; there is no signature, no issuer and no claim structure, although the whitepaper names verifiable credentials and digital wallets. This absence is where Universal Manifest met it cleanly in the project's integration: Universal Manifest signs exactly this content shape byte for byte and adds a signature block beside it, so nothing in the Web of Worlds payload had to change.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Without selective disclosure the traveller over-shares, which is a harm rather than a stop.
note: The Forum's announcement puts selective disclosure at the centre of the design, saying only the data a given experience needs is shared. The machine-readable file offers no way to do that: one GET returns the whole UserManifest object behind one HEAD authorisation check, with no projection, no per-field scope and no consent record.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Content pinned to the Earth must land in the same place in the other system, and a pose that cannot be read puts it somewhere else.
note: Every schema carries a geoPose object shaped like an OGC GeoPose basic yaw-pitch-roll unit, but it is not one: there is no pose identifier, no frame specification, no valid time, and longitude is spelled lan. A reader built for OGC GeoPose 1.0 cannot consume it. The project's integration had to keep a separate OGC GeoPose builder and emit both, with a guard that fails if a payload ever spells longitude correctly; that workaround is local and has no public source.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A frame disagreement is measured in metres or kilometres, not in taste.
note: Latitude, longitude and height are bare numbers with no datum, no ellipsoid and no named reference system, so h has no reference surface. Nothing in the three files names a coordinate reference system, a datum or an Earth model.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: The visitor's app and the device runtime are two independent systems, and if they cannot start an immersive session the visit does not happen.
note: A world can advertise a WebXR session profile as a free string under technology, which is a real declaration point, but the vocabulary of that string is undefined and no session lifecycle is described.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A world that cannot ask what the arriving device can do will guess, and guessing wrong costs quality rather than entry.
note: The nearest field, technology.runtime, describes which engine the world was built with, not what the visiting device can do. Nothing flows from client to world.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: The language a world writes its rules in is its own business and never has to cross.
note: Nothing executable is described. World rules live entirely behind the world's own server; the contract returns data and a web application and defines no behaviour that travels with content.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: An agent with no agreed way to perceive and act in a world it did not come from cannot join it at all.
note: The whitepaper puts autonomous agents alongside people as first-class participants and the Forum's announcement says they follow the same standards and API methods; the machine-readable surface has no agent, no actor type and no way to tell a person from a program.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: The use case names inventory, and items that cannot be read at the destination do not travel with the person.
note: The whitepaper promises wearables, credentials and tokens travelling with the person; the user manifest schema carries three fields and no items list of any kind.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: The use case names preferences, and for a person who depends on comfort and accessibility settings, arriving without them ends the visit.
note: The whitepaper lists preferences and settings inside the shared user manifest and the Forum's announcement repeats the promise; the user manifest API defines none.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Naming content by hash makes an item the same item everywhere; without it copies drift while still loading.
note: Everything is referred to by location. There is no hash anywhere in the three files; the asset API's entity tag is described as a cache validator, not a content identifier a second party can recompute.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Assets reach clients over ordinary web delivery, so agreement here buys scale and cost rather than possibility.
note: Delivery is deliberately plain HTTP: entity tags, conditional requests and content negotiation over registered model types, with authorisation folded into the same HEAD request. There is no caching policy, no tiling and no scale story beyond ordinary web infrastructure.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A reader that cannot tell which version it holds, or what to do with the parts it does not know, breaks on the first update, which is the "no hand fixes" test again.
note: All three files are stamped version 0.0.1 and there is no version negotiation, no deprecation rule and no statement of what a reader should do with a field it does not recognise.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Every other must row is a claim until a shared test says it holds, which is exactly what the meeting asked for.
note: There is no conformance vocabulary at all: no normative keyword appears in any of the three files, and no schema declares a single required property, so an empty object validates as a World, a User, a Node, a Portal, a View and a Spatial descriptor alike; the supplied world schema file is an empty-properties stub. The divergence is no longer hypothetical. The world README says the graph hangs off /wow/scene/, the machine-readable file implements /wow/spatial/{spatialID}/node/{nodeId}, and the project's own reference implementation, simpleWorlds, ships a third OpenAPI file that serves /wow/scene/node/{nodeId} and has no /wow/spatial path at all. The specification and its reference implementation do not agree on where the scene graph lives.

subject: Web of Worlds
capability: World generation from a prompt or an image
interop_reason: A generated place that arrives only as frames to watch still reaches the viewer, but as a recording rather than a world the receiver can open and use.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and making a whole three-dimensional place from a description or a picture is not an act it performs or specifies.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A world continued by a model still reaches a viewer, but only as what the model chooses to show, so the receiver cannot keep it or run it again.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and it never continues a world under a viewer's actions from a learned model; there is no such model here.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: How a system turns photographs into a model is its own method, and what leaves is an ordinary asset the container and geometry rows already carry.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and turning a set of ordinary photographs into a textured three-dimensional model is not among its jobs.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so this row is what geometry encoding is for a mesh: splat content in a named format the receiving tool cannot read does not arrive at all, and re-exporting it is the hand fix the use case forbids.
note: The asset interface negotiates content over twenty-one registered model media types, so the shape of the answer exists and no splat type is among them. There is no registered media type for a Gaussian splat set to negotiate, which is a finding about the registry as much as about this subject.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Without an agreed order for what arrives first, a large capture still loads, it just makes the viewer wait for the whole of it.
note: Delivery is deliberately plain: entity tags, conditional requests and content negotiation. That is enough to fetch a whole asset and says nothing about starting a large capture before all of it has arrived.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a volumetric clip is an asset like any other: without the calibration and mask metadata a second implementation needs, what arrives is not the recording and no one can make it one by hand.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and it carries no captured, time-varying three-dimensional scene as media, and no camera calibration or mask metadata for one.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a point cloud encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a point cloud, exactly as an undecodable mesh is not a mesh, and that capture shows nothing.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and it defines no encoding or compression for a set of points with attributes.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so views that arrive without their intrinsics and extrinsics cannot be reprojected: the capture lands as loose pictures rather than as the place it recorded.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and it carries no set of calibrated camera views with per-pixel depth, and no intrinsics or extrinsics to reproject them.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Making an image from a viewpoint no camera occupied is a method inside one system, and what crosses to a second system is the picture it produced.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and it produces no image from a viewing position that no capture camera occupied.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a moving capture handed over as unrelated frames is not the capture: the receiver has to guess the rate and the ordering the sender already knew, and guessing is the hand fix the use case forbids.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and it carries no captured scene that changes over time, and states no rate at which one should be played back.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Whether a captured scene answers the light around it is work the receiving system does, and the asset arrives either way.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and it holds no captured scene that could be made to answer the light of the place it lands in.

subject: Web of Worlds
capability: Editing a capture after the fact
interop_reason: Editing a capture happens in the tool that holds it, and what leaves is the edited asset, which the format rows already carry.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and there is no capture here to crop, delete from or recolour, and no export for such an edit to survive.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Describing a change to a world you already made is one service's own interface, and the world that results still leaves by the ordinary export rows.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and there is no generated world here to change by describing the change or pointing at a region.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A generator that cannot read the specification another tool wrote still produces a world, it just will not be the world that was asked for.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and nothing here accepts a specification of a world that should be made.

subject: Web of Worlds
capability: Deriving conventional assets from a generated scene
interop_reason: Derived meshes and panoramas are how a generated world reaches a conventional engine at all, and each route loses something the receiver has to be told about.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and it derives no collision mesh, drawing mesh, panorama or video from a splat or radiance-field world.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Actions that arrive without their embodiment, frame and units cannot be replayed elsewhere, so an agent acts only in the system it was written for.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and it carries no agent's actions in or out as time-sampled data with an embodiment, a frame and units.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A panorama whose projection is not stated is still an image, but the receiver has to guess before it can use it as a backdrop or as a light.
note: Web of Worlds is three small OpenAPI files that make a world, its assets and a user manifest addressable over ordinary web protocols, and it carries no full 360-degree view of a place as an image with its projection stated.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A reconstruction that cannot leave the device that made it keeps the room private to one session, so anything placed against it has to be fitted again elsewhere.
note: A framework for addressing and moving between virtual worlds by URI, with the world's own description supplied over its API. Nothing in it comes from a device's sensors, so a live reconstruction of a real room is not something it carries.

subject: Web of Worlds
capability: Semantic labelling of the real world
interop_reason: Labels each vendor names differently still serve one application, but a second one cannot act on floor or sky without being rewritten for that vendor.
note: Its schemas describe worlds, users, assets and presence. There is no field for naming a real floor, wall or object seen through a camera.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Depth reported in units the receiver does not share puts real surfaces at the wrong distance, so content is placed badly rather than not at all.
note: No depth of the physical world appears anywhere in the API. The framework moves world descriptions and user manifests, not sensor readings.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Whether real surfaces hide virtual content is drawn on the device that sees them, and none of that decision crosses to a second system.
note: How a client draws a world, and whether real surfaces hide it, is left entirely to the client. The framework decides addressing and portability, not rendering.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: How much of the real room a runtime lets through is its own presentation, and an arriving asset cannot tell the difference.
note: Web of Worlds describes worlds and the ways in and out of them. How a client presents a world against a camera view of the room is the client's own affair and the API says nothing about it.

subject: Web of Worlds
capability: Face and body tracking as input
interop_reason: A face and body stream in a shape the receiver does not read leaves the avatar still rather than absent, and its privacy terms have to be agreed with it.
note: The API is about a world's description and a visitor's session, not about reading the visitor's face or body from a sensor.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A place that arrives without its walkable surface and arrival points still loads, but whoever opens it has to work out where a body may stand and where a portal lands.
note: A world advertises how it is moved through as one free-text string beside its avatar and gravity settings. That is a hint for a person choosing a world, not a declaration a client can act on: no walkable surface, no bounds, no spawn points, nothing that tells an arriving client where a body may stand.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A published unit of logic whose name resolves to something else elsewhere still runs, but nobody can be sure which code they called.
note: Worlds are addressed by URL and described by a manifest of aspects. Nothing is published as a reusable unit of logic under a name that has to keep resolving, so there is no namespace here and no protection against a second author reusing a name.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A receiving world that cannot tell what review arriving content has already had still shows it, and has to repeat the whole review itself.
note: The API is where a receiving client would learn what a world is before entering it, and the description it gets covers cost, version, duration, technology and presence. There is no content rating, no review record and no statement of who has checked the world or its contents.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: Two maps of one place with no published transform between them put the same content in two positions, so a person arrives beside where they meant to be.
note: A world may carry a GeoPose that puts it somewhere on Earth. That is a placement, not a declared map with a version, and the API publishes no transform between two maps of a place.

subject: Web of Worlds
interop_reason: A service that never declares where it applies still answers, so a client has to call it and find out instead of testing whether it is relevant.
note: The geographic hook is a single GeoPose: one latitude, longitude and height with angles. A point is not an area, so a client cannot test whether a world applies where the client is; it can only be told where the world claims to be.

subject: Web of Worlds

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: How a system turns geometry into pixels never leaves that system, so two runtimes can draw the same scene by different means and nothing crosses.
note: It draws nothing. It is a document format, an evaluation contract and a set of checkers; the specification's whole output is a verdict and a receipt.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The file is the boundary: if the second system cannot open it, nothing else on this list matters.
note: It carries no geometry and no scene. Its relation to a spatial fabric or an asset is a pointer and nothing more, and a pointer is required to carry a type and a target and nothing else.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A signed record of who made an asset lets a receiver trust it; without one the asset still works but nobody can check its history.
note: Universal Manifest signs with Ed25519 over RFC 8785 canonical JSON, bound to a key named by a decentralized identifier. The RP1 fabric it points at signs with a compact JSON Web Signature, RS256 and an X.509 chain. A verifier for one cannot verify the other, and the project's integration resolved that by refusing to merge them: the bridge is a pointer from the manifest to the fabric URL, never a re-signing. They answer different questions, who the person is and who published these bytes, and both are needed. The public specification states the profile; the framing of it as deliberately not a JSON Web Signature, and the bridge decision, are the project's own record.
sources: https://universalmanifest.net/spec/v0.4/core/ | Fabric file entity document, web reader limit (observed, no public source states it)

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The portable description of the body is the artefact this use case moves; with no agreement the person arrives as nothing.
note: Universal Manifest points at an avatar and never describes one. Pointers exist precisely so that heavy files stay where they are, so format, rig, scale and wearables are somebody else's problem by declaration.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Without a way to bind an avatar to a verifiable identity, the person who arrives cannot be shown to be the person who left.
note: The binding is real but it is generic, and a working group should know which half is standardised. The specification defines a typed pointer array: every pointer must carry a type and a target, the pointers sit inside the bytes the signature covers, and an evaluator meeting a pointer type it does not recognise must record it and must not act on it. It names no avatar pointer. The avatar meaning comes from a published fixture set and from a third-party implementation, both of which use the pointer name portableIdentity.avatar. So a destination can check that this person really claims this avatar, and it learns nothing about what the avatar file contains.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: With no shared wire protocol there is no session to join at all.
note: Explicitly not a host, a store or a transport. The envelope is fetched over whatever the deployment uses and the specification is careful to keep transport out: it notes that two devices may exchange manifests over a local link such as near-field, Bluetooth or a printed code and each verify the other without a server.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Joining a running world, authentication included, is the door: no agreement, no entry.
note: The base model still evaluates at a boundary: a document arrives, six stages run in order, a receipt is written, and nothing in the base re-checks anything while an interaction is running. A bilateral session model does exist but it is carried in the optional-features profile and marked preview. That matters because the gap has now been filled from the other side: TeleportXR, which lives entirely in the during-session layer, has shipped a message that invalidates an accepted avatar mid-session, and nothing on this side is specified to drive it.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: This row is the portal itself, and the travel use case is nothing but the handoff.
note: The envelope is the state that crosses the boundary, and the specification supplies the general machinery: facets, claims, consents and pointers inside one signed document that a destination evaluates on arrival. What crossed in practice, pose, session, equipment, a continuity identifier and fifteen manifest facets between two separate world servers, together with the fail-closed gate that decided whether traversal was allowed at all, is the project's own working crossing and has no public source. What it did not carry was velocity, and it performed no scale or precision change.
sources: https://universalmanifest.net/spec/v0.4/core/ | Open Spatial Lab design note, precision domain (observed composition failure, no public source states it)

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A destination name that does not resolve cannot be travelled to, so naming and resolution are the first agreement.
note: A manifest is fetched from an address, or resolved from a short identifier by a hosted resolver, and the manifest points onward at the things it describes. The resolver is a locator and nothing more: a third-party implementation records that although the resolver serves a one-minute HTTP cache header, consumers must enforce the manifest's own lifetime regardless of HTTP caching, so resolution and trust stay separate steps.
sources: https://universalmanifest.net/ | Spatial fabric ecosystem map, typology catalog

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: With no shared base identifier the same person or agent is a stranger in every world they enter.
note: The signature block names its verification key by URI reference and the specification requires that reference to be present, recommending a decentralized identifier URL or an HTTPS URL. An embedded public key may travel beside it for offline verification, but the reference itself must still resolve. A third-party implementation states the reason plainly: accepting an inline key without checking it against the reference is exactly what would let an attacker re-sign a modified document with their own key.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Claims about age, membership or ownership are worthless if the receiving world cannot read them.
note: This is the subject's core and it is now published in full. Signature Profile A is the baseline normative profile: RFC 8785 canonical JSON with the signature member removed, signed with Ed25519, the value base64url without padding. The evaluator checklist is ordered and mandatory, and a manifest whose only signature uses an unsupported profile is rejected rather than accepted quietly. The context document is pinned by its own content hash, so the meaning of the terms cannot be swapped underneath a verifier.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A credential nobody can ask for or present is not a credential, and one subject reaches this row natively today.
note: The base model is still an evaluation of a presented document rather than an interactive request-and-present protocol, and the interactive parts, holder binding and presentation proof, live in a companion profile with several sections still marked preview. But the older reading of this row, that the three specifications it would present to all leave the slot empty and no plug is specified, is no longer true. One of the three now has a plug: the public TeleportXR repository accepts a manifest address in place of an avatar URL, resolves it, verifies Signature Profile A, and answers with a receipt. A live replay weakness found in the project's own reciprocal-control holder binding, and fixed locally by binding the full content hash, was never delivered upstream; that remains a project-local record.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A world that cannot read what an arriving person or agent is allowed to do must either refuse it or trust it blindly.
note: Permission is expressed as consent records inside the signed envelope, each naming the operations it allows, the purpose it allows them for, and a validity window; a separate pointer type declares delegated session authority for an agent. The evaluation rule is default-deny and it is normative: a facet with no consent entry governing it is recorded as consent-missing, and an evaluator must not process facet data when required consent is absent, expired or withdrawn. Every decision, allow or refuse, is recorded in a structured receipt.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Without selective disclosure the traveller over-shares, which is a harm rather than a stop.
note: Selective disclosure is a normative stage of the evaluation sequence rather than an add-on: the evaluator must extract only the facets, claims, pointers and device entries relevant to its processing context, and the specification calls this the bounded selective minimum disclosure profile. Beneath it sit encrypted facets, sealed with JSON Web Encryption inside the envelope, where a facet the evaluator cannot open must be acknowledged as present but unread rather than guessed at or treated as a failure. The stronger tracks, zero-knowledge proofs and unlinkable disclosure, are published as preview and should not be counted as shipping.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Relationships and standing that do not travel leave the person present but unknown.
note: Standing between parties is expressed, a relationship graph is not. The optional-features profile defines a typed trust weight and category trust, and a bilateral session model where two parties each evaluate the other and each keeps a receipt. There is no follower model, no portable contact list and no social graph of any kind.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The terms themselves must cross, and that row is a must; acting on them is the receiver's own behaviour, and no agreed mechanism exists yet.
note: Terms are acted on at the point of use, but the terms are consents rather than licences: an operation outside the granted scope, or a use outside the declared purpose, is refused and recorded, and an expired or withdrawn grant is treated as absent. There is no licence vocabulary and no enforcement of asset rights. The worked example of a denied cross-world link keeping a link local is the project's own integration and has no public source.
sources: https://universalmanifest.net/spec/v0.4/core/ | RP1 entity document, delivery observation (observed, no public source states the CORS posture)

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Content pinned to the Earth must land in the same place in the other system, and a pose that cannot be read puts it somewhere else.
note: This row previously claimed a working geographic pose and that was too generous. The published specification lists a GeoPose primary pose value profile among its design-stage candidate profiles, marked preview and not yet on the wire, and states that the candidate members are absent from the published schema, context and fixtures until finalized. The published v0.4 context confirms it: none of its terms names a pose, a coordinate, a geographic frame or a spatial anchor. The spatial bookmarks pairing a fabric identifier with a pose exist in this project's own material and not in the specification.
sources: https://universalmanifest.net/spec/v0.4/core/ | https://universalmanifest.net/spec/v0.4/ext-opt/ | https://universalmanifest.net/ns/v0.4 | Universal Manifest entity document, section 1

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: An agent with no agreed way to perceive and act in a world it did not come from cannot join it at all.
note: Agents are a first-class subject of the envelope rather than an afterthought. A manifest's subject may be a person, an agent, a device or an organisation; a pointer type declares delegated session authority, so an agent can carry evidence that it acts for someone; and the scope vocabulary in the optional-features profile includes participating in a spatial session on the subject's behalf. What is not here is any agent behaviour, lifecycle or runtime; the envelope says who is acting and under what authority, and stops there.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The use case names inventory, and items that cannot be read at the destination do not travel with the person.
note: The envelope is the natural carrier for carried items and the general machinery is there, typed facets and typed pointers inside the signed bytes, but the specification defines no inventory, no item list and no equipment vocabulary. The project's working crossing did move an equipped-items list with the person; that list is a project-local profile with its own version string and the research record says plainly it is not a standards claim until the exact schema version is fixed.
sources: https://universalmanifest.net/spec/v0.4/core/ | Universal Manifest source note | Open Spatial Lab portal traversal controller

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: The use case names preferences, and for a person who depends on comfort and accessibility settings, arriving without them ends the visit.
note: What follows the person is policy, not settings. Consent records travel inside the signed envelope, each carrying the operations it permits, the purpose it permits them for and its validity window, so a person's standing decisions about use are portable and are re-evaluated at every destination. Accessibility choices and rendering preferences are not modelled at all: the specification has no preference vocabulary. The spatial bookmarks described elsewhere in this project are its own profile and are not in the published context.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Naming content by hash makes an item the same item everywhere; without it copies drift while still loading.
note: One thing is addressed by hash and it is the right one: the JSON-LD context document is named by a content hash, that hash is normative for context integrity, and the optional-features profile fixes the hash function as SHA-256 in multihash form. So the meaning of every term in the envelope is pinned to exact bytes. The envelope's own pointers out to heavy files remain plain locations; the base pointer requires a target URI and does not require a digest.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A runnable experience moves between hosts far less often than an asset does, and repackaging is the fallback.
note: Declared pointer-only. The envelope never packages a runnable experience and never hosts one: pointers exist so that heavy files and records stay outside the handshake, and the project describes itself as an open specification rather than a platform.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A reader that cannot tell which version it holds, or what to do with the parts it does not know, breaks on the first update, which is the "no hand fixes" test again.
note: Versioning is explicit and the honesty about its cost is unusual. Each version has its own document set, its own context URL and its own conformance fixtures, v0.3 is named as the stable published reference and v0.4 as the production-candidate milestone, and the specification states outright that while the line is still 0.x a minor bump may include breaking changes in a new version folder. So a reader can always tell which vocabulary it is holding. What there is not is a negotiation mechanism or a deprecation policy: an evaluator either accepts a context value or does not.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Every other must row is a claim until a shared test says it holds, which is exactly what the meeting asked for.
note: The one subject in this group with a written specification and a real conformance suite, and both are public. Requirement keywords are used under BCP 14, the evaluation sequence names the six stages an evaluator must run in order and requires a structured receipt for every processed manifest, and fixture suites are published per version with valid cases, invalid cases and an expected-results file. One finding a standards audience will want, and it is the project's own and was never reported upstream: the implementation's canonicalizer turned out to follow RFC 8785 more closely than the specification's own reference canonicalizer.

subject: Universal Manifest
capability: World generation from a prompt or an image
interop_reason: A generated place that arrives only as frames to watch still reaches the viewer, but as a recording rather than a world the receiver can open and use.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and making a whole three-dimensional place from a description or a picture is not an act it performs or specifies.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A world continued by a model still reaches a viewer, but only as what the model chooses to show, so the receiver cannot keep it or run it again.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and it never continues a world under a viewer's actions from a learned model; there is no such model here.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: How a system turns photographs into a model is its own method, and what leaves is an ordinary asset the container and geometry rows already carry.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and turning a set of ordinary photographs into a textured three-dimensional model is not among its jobs.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so this row is what geometry encoding is for a mesh: splat content in a named format the receiving tool cannot read does not arrive at all, and re-exporting it is the hand fix the use case forbids.
note: The manifest names a resource by pointer and never inspects it, so a splat file is exactly as opaque to it as a photograph. Its own site states the design: heavy files stay where they are.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Without an agreed order for what arrives first, a large capture still loads, it just makes the viewer wait for the whole of it.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and it delivers no captured scene, progressively by region and detail or otherwise.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a volumetric clip is an asset like any other: without the calibration and mask metadata a second implementation needs, what arrives is not the recording and no one can make it one by hand.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and it carries no captured, time-varying three-dimensional scene as media, and no camera calibration or mask metadata for one.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a point cloud encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a point cloud, exactly as an undecodable mesh is not a mesh, and that capture shows nothing.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and it defines no encoding or compression for a set of points with attributes.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so views that arrive without their intrinsics and extrinsics cannot be reprojected: the capture lands as loose pictures rather than as the place it recorded.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and it carries no set of calibrated camera views with per-pixel depth, and no intrinsics or extrinsics to reproject them.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Making an image from a viewpoint no camera occupied is a method inside one system, and what crosses to a second system is the picture it produced.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and it produces no image from a viewing position that no capture camera occupied.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Captured content is first-class, so a moving capture handed over as unrelated frames is not the capture: the receiver has to guess the rate and the ordering the sender already knew, and guessing is the hand fix the use case forbids.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and it carries no captured scene that changes over time, and states no rate at which one should be played back.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Whether a captured scene answers the light around it is work the receiving system does, and the asset arrives either way.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and it holds no captured scene that could be made to answer the light of the place it lands in.

subject: Universal Manifest
capability: Editing a capture after the fact
interop_reason: Editing a capture happens in the tool that holds it, and what leaves is the edited asset, which the format rows already carry.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and there is no capture here to crop, delete from or recolour, and no export for such an edit to survive.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Describing a change to a world you already made is one service's own interface, and the world that results still leaves by the ordinary export rows.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and there is no generated world here to change by describing the change or pointing at a region.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A generator that cannot read the specification another tool wrote still produces a world, it just will not be the world that was asked for.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and nothing here accepts a specification of a world that should be made.

subject: Universal Manifest
capability: Deriving conventional assets from a generated scene
interop_reason: Derived meshes and panoramas are how a generated world reaches a conventional engine at all, and each route loses something the receiver has to be told about.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and it derives no collision mesh, drawing mesh, panorama or video from a splat or radiance-field world.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Actions that arrive without their embodiment, frame and units cannot be replayed elsewhere, so an agent acts only in the system it was written for.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and it carries no agent's actions in or out as time-sampled data with an embodiment, a frame and units.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A panorama whose projection is not stated is still an image, but the receiver has to guess before it can use it as a backdrop or as a light.
note: Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope that points at heavy things rather than carrying them, and it carries no full 360-degree view of a place as an image with its projection stated.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A reconstruction that cannot leave the device that made it keeps the room private to one session, so anything placed against it has to be fitted again elsewhere.
note: A manifest that points at assets and declares what they are, composing with other standards rather than replacing them. It describes prepared content, not a live reading of the room around a device.

subject: Universal Manifest
capability: Semantic labelling of the real world
interop_reason: Labels each vendor names differently still serve one application, but a second one cannot act on floor or sky without being rewritten for that vendor.
note: Its vocabulary names the parts of a declared experience. Nothing in it labels a real surface a camera has seen.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Depth reported in units the receiver does not share puts real surfaces at the wrong distance, so content is placed badly rather than not at all.
note: No depth channel exists. The manifest carries pointers and metadata, and heavy data stays where it lives.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Whether real surfaces hide virtual content is drawn on the device that sees them, and none of that decision crosses to a second system.
note: Drawing is not the manifest's business at all, so how virtual content sits against real surfaces is outside it.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: How much of the real room a runtime lets through is its own presentation, and an arriving asset cannot tell the difference.
note: The manifest is evaluated before anything is shown. It carries no presentation control, so how a viewer blends a camera view of the room is outside it.

subject: Universal Manifest
capability: Face and body tracking as input
interop_reason: A face and body stream in a shape the receiver does not read leaves the avatar still rather than absent, and its privacy terms have to be agreed with it.
note: Universal Manifest speaks about consent for sensor-derived data rather than delivering a stream: no face or body pose reaches an application through it.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A place that arrives without its walkable surface and arrival points still loads, but whoever opens it has to work out where a body may stand and where a portal lands.
note: The manifest describes trust, consent and policy for a piece of content, not the shape of a place, so walkable surface and arrival points are outside it.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A published unit of logic whose name resolves to something else elsewhere still runs, but nobody can be sure which code they called.
note: The only permanent name in the specification is its own: a versioned namespace URI that says which version of the manifest schema a document conforms to. Nothing names a published unit of world logic, so no author can depend on a name here and no name is protected from a second claimant.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A receiving world that cannot tell what review arriving content has already had still shows it, and has to repeat the whole review itself.
note: This is the closest thing on the map to the interoperable half of the row: content arrives with a manifest, and a six-stage evaluation — arrive, verify, project, consent, compose, receipt — runs before it is composed into the receiving surface, leaving a receipt behind. It is a trust and consent gate rather than a content review: nothing in it says who looked at the content, what they judged, or that a review happened at all.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: Two maps of one place with no published transform between them put the same content in two positions, so a person arrives beside where they meant to be.
note: The specification's only geographic idea is a candidate profile carrying GeoPose values, and even that is drafted rather than on the wire. It declares no map of a place and no transform between two maps.

subject: Universal Manifest
interop_reason: A service that never declares where it applies still answers, so a client has to call it and find out instead of testing whether it is relevant.
note: A manifest travels with content and describes its trust conditions, not an area of the Earth where a service or dataset applies.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: An asset that arrives against a different surface model still loads, but the further apart the two models are the more the look drifts.
note: VRMC_materials_mtoon 1.0 defines a toon surface model with shade colour, shading shift and toony factor, matcap and parametric rim light, an outline mode and an explicit render queue. It sits alongside the glTF material rather than replacing it.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Authored viewpoints are part of a scene, and losing them costs the arrival shot, not the scene.
note: VRM removes glTF cameras from use, then defines the one viewpoint an avatar needs: the wearer's own. Meshes are annotated third person only, first person only, both or auto, and the auto rule splits a mesh by head bone weight so the wearer does not see the inside of their own face. Missing: no camera definition, no viewpoint binding, no way to move between viewpoints.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: A disagreement about handedness or axis order puts every object in the wrong place or mirrored, which is the classic hand fix.
note: Handedness and axis order come from glTF and VRM restates none of it. VRM does add the convention glTF lacks for characters: in the rest pose the model stands facing positive Z, symmetrical about X, arms out along X, and every node scale must be uniform and positive. Missing: no transform convention of its own beyond the rest pose.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: The file is the boundary: if the second system cannot open it, nothing else on this list matters.
note: Defines its own file: binary glTF with a required VRMC_vrm extension carrying specVersion, humanoid and meta, saved with the .vrm suffix. The container is glTF's; what makes it a VRM is the required extension.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: A mesh encoded in a way the receiver cannot decode is not a mesh, and the compression choice is where this usually breaks.
note: Mesh encoding is glTF's and VRM specifies none of it. What VRM adds is two restrictions aimed at making models load the same everywhere: stored tangents may be left out and recalculated, and morph target tangents should be neither exported nor imported.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Device-specific texture compression is the common failure: the model arrives untextured and someone must re-export it.
note: Image encoding is glTF's. VRM adds one restriction and it is a narrow one: the model thumbnail must be square and must be a jpg or png supported by glTF's core, with extension formats forbidden. Missing: nothing is said about texture compression for the model's own textures.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Carrying materials without loss is what "renders in another system" means, and only two subjects reach this row natively today.
note: A VRM model keeps its glTF core material, so a plain physically based renderer will show something. What will not carry is the intended look: the toon material is defined by reference to particular rendering techniques, so shade colour, rim light, matcap and outline are reproduced only by a renderer that implements the extension.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: A clip that cannot be read leaves the object still, and an avatar that cannot move is not an avatar.
note: A VRM file carries no animation: the core says the glTF animations and cameras arrays are not used. Humanoid motion lives in a separate file defined by VRMC_vrm_animation 1.0, which reuses glTF's own keyframe machinery and adds the mapping to named bones, expressions and gaze.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: The bone hierarchy is what makes a body move correctly elsewhere; without an agreed one, motion has nothing to bind to.
note: Binding and skinning are glTF's; the part VRM adds is the mapping from each named human bone to a glTF node, which is what makes the rig readable by a runtime that never saw the model. Bone transforms are constrained further: scale must be uniform and positive.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Blend shapes carry facial detail, so losing them freezes a face rather than stopping the transfer.
note: The shape deformation itself is glTF's morph targets, which VRM does not change. What VRM adds is naming: expressions bind groups of morph targets to an agreed name, and because glTF has no name for a morph target the specification recommends putting one in the mesh extras. Missing: VRM specifies no encoding of its own.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Layered references are a working convenience, and flattening on export is the fallback that keeps the asset moving.
note: A VRM file is one self-contained humanoid. There is no referencing another file, no layering and no override, which is the structural reason a wearable cannot be shipped separately from the avatar it is worn on.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: A metre read as a centimetre makes the asset useless on arrival, and rescaling by hand is the fix the use case forbids.
note: Metric scale is inherited from glTF. VRM adds the rule that makes avatar size and grounding usable: the sole surface sits on the plane at Y zero in appearance, so a receiving world can place the feet and read the height without guessing where the ankle bone is. Missing: the unit agreement itself is glTF's.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: An item that arrives with no readable terms cannot be lawfully worn, shown or sold, so the move fails at the rights boundary even when every byte arrives.
note: Unusual for a 3D format and the reason VRM matters to the rights columns. The meta block requires a name, at least one author and a licence document link that must point at the VRM Public License, and then adds eleven machine-readable settings: who may act as this avatar, commercial use, credit, redistribution, modification, and flags for violent, sexual, political or religious, and antisocial or hateful use. Every default is the restrictive one.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: A signed record of who made an asset lets a receiver trust it; without one the asset still works but nobody can check its history.
note: Authorship is recorded and required: authors, and optionally copyright holder, contact, references to original works, and third party licences. Missing is the whole verifiable half. Nothing is signed, there is no issuer and no way for a recipient to tell a true author field from an invented one.

interop_reason: Agreed bone names are what let animation authored anywhere play on the arriving body.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: The use case names expressions, and named shapes the destination does not know leave a blank face.
note: 18 named preset expressions: happy, angry, sad, relaxed, surprised; the mouth shapes aa, ih, ou, ee, oh; blink, blinkLeft, blinkRight; lookUp, lookDown, lookLeft, lookRight; and neutral. Custom names are allowed but may not reuse a preset name. The trap is that only the names are agreed, not the faces.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Retargeting is the repair when skeletons differ, so its absence costs motion quality rather than the visit.
note: The named bone set and the normative rest pose in the core are what let motion move between bodies; the portable motion file itself is a separate extension, VRMC_vrm_animation 1.0. What is missing is normative force for the hard part: the rules for reconciling models with different rest rotations and different optional bones sit in a document the project marks as non-normative.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Equipped items are named in the use case, and attachment points that do not survive leave items on the floor or on the wrong bone.
note: VRM defines no worn item, no attachment point and no socket. Clothing, hats and held props must be part of the avatar's own mesh hierarchy before export; the only thing an implementation can hang an item on is the named bone set, and nothing in the specification says how. The spring bone extension mentions costumes only as something that should sway.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Reduced forms matter for crowds and weak devices, and their absence costs frames, not presence.
note: No reduced avatar representation of any kind. The nearest thing, the first-person mesh annotation, switches whole meshes on and off per camera to keep the wearer's own head out of their view; it does not reduce detail and does not help with crowds or weak devices.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Without a way to bind an avatar to a verifiable identity, the person who arrives cannot be shown to be the person who left.
note: Nothing ties a VRM file to a person or a credential. The meta block names authors as free text and offers contact information, but there is no identifier, no signature and no way to check that the named author made the file.

subject: VRM
interop_reason: Cloth and hair are the visible part, so a moved avatar arrives stiff rather than absent.

There is no cloth solver, no mesh deformation, branching chains are undefined, and two runtimes stepping at different rates will not match.
